distractorNotes.d: Subagents are not metered outside the run. Each subagent issues its own API requests, and those requests count toward the same total cost the budget cap is compared against, which is exactly why the cap is useful for bounding a run that fans out.
distractorNotes.e: The result text is available on a successful completion. On a run that ends at a limit, the subtype reports which limit was hit and no final result text is available, so code that reads the result field unconditionally will find nothing there.

sourceNote: Sections 'Control how the loop runs' subsection 'Turns and budget', and 'Handle the result'
scopeNote: Agent architecture is in scope, but the options separate on exact SDK metering rules, specifically that maximum-turns counts tool-use turns only. That is a documented constant rather than a design principle.

stem: An Agent SDK agent is given a formatting rule in its opening prompt. It follows the rule early on, but many turns into the same long session it quietly stops applying it, even though no options or prompts were changed. What explains this, and what is the documented way to make the rule stick?

options.text: The context window is cleared between turns once a session grows long, so any instruction has to be repeated in each new prompt the application sends rather than being stated once at the start of the session.

The SDK lowers the reasoning effort level automatically as a session lengthens, and the rule will be honoured again once effort is raised back to the value the session started with, without any change to the prompt.

Automatic compaction replaced older history with a summary that dropped the rule; durable instructions belong in a project CLAUDE.md loaded through setting sources, since that content is supplied on every request.
Instructions given to the main agent stop applying once tool use begins, so the rule has to be moved into the system prompt of a subagent that performs the formatting step on the main agent's behalf.

explanation: Context accumulates across a session rather than resetting: the system prompt, tool definitions, conversation history, and every tool input and output all build up. When the window approaches its limit, the SDK compacts the conversation by summarizing older history while keeping recent exchanges and key decisions. Compaction is lossy by design, so a specific instruction stated once at the start of a long session may not survive the summary. CLAUDE.md is treated differently because its content is supplied on every request, which is why persistent rules belong there rather than in a one-time opening prompt. A pre-compaction hook can also run custom logic before a summary is produced.

distractorNotes.a: The context window explicitly does not reset between turns within a session; everything accumulates. That accumulation is the reason compaction exists at all.
distractorNotes.b: Effort is a configuration value controlling how much reasoning Claude applies per response. The SDK does not decay it over the life of a session, and raising it would not restore content a summary dropped.
distractorNotes.d: Main-agent instructions remain in force across tool use. Moving the rule into a subagent would confine it to that subagent's isolated context, which is the opposite of making it apply to the whole session.

sourceNote: Section 'The context window', subsections 'What consumes context' and 'Automatic compaction'

stem: Anthropic's published guidance on building effective agents treats both workflows and agents as agentic systems, but draws an architectural distinction between them. What is that distinction?

options.text: A workflow coordinates several different models and routes between them, whereas an agent is restricted to a single model for the whole of its run.
In a workflow, model calls and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths; in an agent, the model dynamically directs its own process and tool usage.
An agent is able to call tools and use retrieval, whereas a workflow can only chain model calls together and pass text from one step to the next.
A workflow pauses for human approval at every step, whereas an agent runs from start to finish with no human involvement once it has been given its task and the tools it needs.

explanation: The distinction turns on who determines the sequence of steps. In a workflow the path is fixed in advance by code the developer writes, which yields predictability and consistency for well-defined tasks. In an agent the model decides what to do next and which tools to use as it goes, which buys flexibility for problems whose steps cannot be enumerated ahead of time. The same guidance recommends reaching for the simplest option that works, since agentic systems trade latency and cost for task performance and many applications are served well by a single optimized model call with retrieval and good examples.

distractorNotes.a: The number of models involved is orthogonal to the distinction. A workflow may route between models of different sizes as a cost optimization, and an agent can be built on a single model.
distractorNotes.c: Both categories build on a model augmented with capabilities such as tools, retrieval, and memory. Workflows call tools too; the difference is that those calls sit on a path defined by code.
distractorNotes.d: Human oversight is a separate design choice. Agents commonly return to a human for judgement at checkpoints or when blocked, and workflows can run start to finish without approval steps.

sourceNote: Sections 'What are agents?' and 'When (and when not) to use agents'

stem: A code-modification feature must change a set of files that differs with every request, and neither the number of files nor the nature of each change can be known before the request arrives. The design has one central model call break the request into subtasks at runtime, hand each subtask to a worker model call, and combine the workers' output into a single answer. Which documented agentic pattern does this describe?

options.text: Parallelization using sectioning
Evaluator-optimizer
Prompt chaining
Orchestrator-workers

explanation: Orchestrator-workers suits tasks whose subtasks cannot be predicted in advance. A central model call decomposes the work for the specific input it received, delegates the pieces to workers, and synthesizes their results. Coding changes that touch an unpredictable number of files are the example the guidance itself gives. The pattern is structurally similar to parallelization, and the stated difference is precisely the one this scenario turns on: the subtasks are determined by the orchestrator at runtime rather than fixed by the developer beforehand.

distractorNotes.a: Sectioning splits a task into independent subtasks the developer has defined ahead of time and runs them concurrently. It is the closest structural match, but it presumes the breakdown is known before the input arrives, which is what this scenario rules out.
distractorNotes.b: Evaluator-optimizer pairs a generator with a critic that reviews its output and feeds back suggestions in a loop. It suits work with clear evaluation criteria that benefits from iterative refinement, not work that must fan out across an unknown number of files.
distractorNotes.c: Prompt chaining decomposes a task into a fixed sequence of steps in which each call processes the previous call's output, optionally with programmatic gates between steps. It depends on the decomposition being clean and known in advance.

sourceNote: Section 'Building blocks, workflows, and agents', subsection 'Workflow: Orchestrator-workers'

stem: A team is deciding between having Claude delegate to subagents turn by turn and running the same job as a dynamic workflow. Which statement correctly captures the documented difference between the two approaches?

options.text: The two are the same mechanism in every respect except for scale: a dynamic workflow raises the ceiling on how many subagents may run at once, so a job that saturates that limit finishes sooner when expressed as a workflow instead.

In a dynamic workflow a script owns the loop, the branching, and the intermediate results, so only the final answer reaches Claude's context; with subagents Claude decides what to spawn turn by turn and every result returns into its window.

Subagents are dispatched one after another and each must finish before the next one begins, so a dynamic workflow is the only one of the two approaches that can execute independent branches of the same job concurrently rather than in sequence.

A dynamic workflow keeps every agent's full transcript in the main conversation so that the run can be audited end to end, whereas subagents discard their transcripts and return only a final message to the parent when they finish.

explanation: The two approaches differ in who holds the plan. With subagents, Claude is the orchestrator and decides turn by turn what to delegate, and every returned result occupies space in its context window. A dynamic workflow moves the plan into a script the runtime executes, so control flow and intermediate values live in script variables instead. That shift is what allows a workflow to coordinate far more agents per run than one conversation can, and it also makes the orchestration itself repeatable, since the script can be reread, rerun, and saved for later use.

distractorNotes.a: The difference is not a quota. Raising a concurrency ceiling would still leave Claude deciding each delegation turn by turn and still leave every result accumulating in its context, which is the specific constraint a workflow removes.
distractorNotes.c: Subagents can run concurrently, and running independent subtasks in parallel is one of their stated benefits. Concurrency is not what separates the two approaches.
distractorNotes.d: This inverts the design. Keeping intermediate results out of the main context is the point of a workflow, and a subagent likewise returns only its final message to the parent rather than its full transcript.

sourceNote: Section 'When to use a workflow'

stem: A developer defines a research subagent programmatically and notices it keeps asking about a configuration file the main agent had already read and discussed earlier in the run. For a subagent that is not a fork of the parent conversation, what does the subagent actually receive from the parent?

options.text: The parent's full conversation history with tool results stripped out, so the subagent sees what was said but not what was read from disk or returned by any tool.
The parent's system prompt plus its most recent turns, so the subagent starts with recent context and only the older history is left behind when the delegation begins.
Every skill already preloaded into the parent's context, together with its tool definitions, so the subagent inherits the parent's working knowledge without having to be told about it.
Only the prompt string passed in the Agent tool call, alongside the subagent's own system prompt, project CLAUDE.md loaded through setting sources, and its tool definitions.

explanation: A subagent that is not a fork starts a fresh conversation. Its context is not empty, because it loads its own system prompt, project instruction files, and tool definitions, but none of the parent's conversation crosses over. The only content the parent passes is the prompt string in the Agent tool call, which is why file paths, error messages, and prior decisions the subagent needs must be written into that prompt explicitly. The boundary is deliberately narrow in both directions: intermediate tool calls and results stay inside the subagent, and only its final message returns to the parent as the tool result. That is what makes subagents effective for context isolation.

distractorNotes.a: No portion of the parent's conversation history is transferred, with or without tool results. Assuming otherwise is the specific mistake that produces subagents which appear to have forgotten what the main agent knows.
distractorNotes.b: Neither the parent's system prompt nor its recent turns are inherited. The subagent runs under its own system prompt, which is what lets it carry specialized instructions the main agent does not need.
distractorNotes.c: Preloaded skill content is not inherited. A subagent definition can name skills to preload for that subagent, and unlisted skills remain invocable through the skill tool, but nothing carries across from the parent automatically.

sourceNote: Section 'What subagents inherit'

stem: A team defines a read-only code-review subagent programmatically through the SDK's agents option. Select TWO statements that accurately describe how that agent definition works.

options.text: Omitting the tool list leaves the subagent with no tools at all, so the field must always be populated before the agent can do any work on its own.
A description and a system prompt are the only required fields; the tool list, the model override, and the remaining fields are all optional.

Restricting a subagent's tools only takes effect if a matching deny rule is also configured for the session, since the tool list by itself makes no permission decision and is treated as advisory metadata.
A subagent must exist as a markdown file in a .claude/agents directory before it can be invoked, and the agents option only points at definitions already on disk.
The description field is used only for logging and has no bearing on when Claude chooses to use the subagent, which depends on its system prompt instead.
When the definition lists specific tools, a tool left off that list is absent from the subagent's session entirely, so Claude works without it rather than hitting a permission prompt.

explanation: A subagent definition needs a description telling Claude when to use the agent and a prompt defining how the agent behaves. Everything else, including the tool list, model override, preloaded skills, and per-agent turn or effort settings, is optional. Tool restriction works by shaping the subagent's tool set rather than by intercepting calls: a tool that is not in the list is not part of that session, so there is nothing for Claude to attempt and nothing to deny. That is a meaningfully different mechanism from a deny rule, which leaves the tool visible and produces a denial the model can observe and react to.

distractorNotes.a: Omitting the tool list has the opposite effect: the subagent inherits every tool available to subagents. The field narrows a default-broad tool set rather than opting into one.
distractorNotes.c: The tool list stands on its own. It determines which tool definitions exist in the subagent's session, independently of the allow and deny rules that govern permission decisions for tools that do exist.
distractorNotes.d: Subagents can be defined programmatically through the agents option with no files on disk, and that approach is the recommended one for SDK applications. Filesystem definitions are an alternative, and a programmatic definition takes precedence over a file-based one with the same name.
distractorNotes.e: The description is what Claude matches against when deciding whether a task suits this subagent, so a vague description directly degrades automatic invocation. Naming the agent in the prompt is the way to force a specific one.

sourceNote: Sections 'Create subagents', 'AgentDefinition configuration', 'Invoke subagents', and 'Tool restrictions'
scopeNote: Requires recalling which fields of a programmatic agent definition are required and which are optional. Field-level recall sits above the sample questions' level.

stem: An audit task issued as a single prompt has grown into a tree of subagents that are themselves spawning subagents, and the run costs far more than expected. How does the Agent SDK expose the documented limits on subagent spawn depth, on how many subagents run at once, and on total spend?

options.text: Spawn depth and concurrent subagent count are set as environment variables supplied through the SDK's environment option, while total spend is a query option on the run.
All three are fields on the individual agent definition, so each subagent carries its own depth, concurrency, and spend ceiling alongside its tools and its model.
All three are query options on the run, set alongside the maximum-turns option when the query starts, so one options object caps depth, concurrency, and spend together.
The maximum-turns option covers all three, because every subagent a run spawns consumes one of the run's turns and the run stops once that budget is exhausted.

explanation: Claude decides on its own when to delegate and how many subagents to spawn, and a subagent can spawn further subagents, so one prompt can expand into a tree. The three controls that bound that growth are not exposed uniformly. Nesting depth and the number of subagents running simultaneously are read from environment variables, which you supply through the environment option when starting the run. Total spend is a query option compared against the run's cumulative cost, and because subagent requests are included in that cost it is the control that bounds the tree as a whole. Knowing which control lives where matters, because a spend cap alone will not stop a run from spawning a wide tree, and depth and concurrency limits alone will not cap what the run costs.

distractorNotes.b: The agent definition configures one agent's behaviour, such as its tools, model, and its own turn limit. Depth and concurrency are properties of the run as a whole, since they govern relationships between agents rather than any single agent.
distractorNotes.c: Only the spend cap is a query option. Treating depth and concurrency as query options is the most common form of this mistake and quietly leaves both at their defaults.
distractorNotes.d: The turn limit counts tool-use round trips within the run, not the number of agents spawned, and it says nothing about how deeply subagents nest or how many run at the same time.

sourceNote: Section 'Cap subagent depth, concurrency, and spend'
scopeNote: Requires recalling where each limit is configured, environment variable versus query option. The distinction is a lookup, not a design judgement.

stem: An SDK application must run a compliance check before every tool call, and the check must not be bypassable by configuration made elsewhere in the application. Select TWO statements that correctly describe how the SDK evaluates permissions.

options.text: A pre-tool-use hook runs before deny rules, ask rules, the permission mode, and allow rules, and a denial returned by a hook applies even in bypassPermissions mode.
A hook that returns an allow decision short-circuits the remaining evaluation, so deny rules, ask rules, and the permission mode are no longer consulted for that call.

Naming tools in the allowed-tools list constrains bypassPermissions mode so that only the tools named there are approved, and anything left off the list still reaches the approval callback for a decision before it can run.
In dontAsk mode the tool-approval callback is still invoked for anything that was not pre-approved, so a check placed in that callback continues to run under that mode.
Deny rules are not applied while bypassPermissions mode is active, because that mode is consulted before any rule matching happens and approves the call outright.

Because the tool-approval callback is the last step, a call already resolved by an earlier step, such as a bare allow entry or a permissive mode, never reaches it, so a check placed only there does not run.

explanation: Permission evaluation runs in a fixed order: hooks first, then deny rules, then ask rules, then the permission mode, then allow rules, and finally the tool-approval callback for anything still unresolved. Two consequences follow for a check that must be unconditional. First, a pre-tool-use hook is the only step that sees every call before any other step can resolve it, and a denial from a hook holds even under the most permissive mode. Second, the approval callback sits last and is consulted only when nothing earlier resolved the call, so a broad allow entry or a permissive mode approves the call before the callback is reached. A narrow set of calls that inherently require user interaction is routed to the callback regardless, but that exception cannot be relied on to enforce a general policy, which is why the hook is the documented place for one.

distractorNotes.b: An allow decision from a hook does not skip the steps below it. Deny and ask rules are evaluated regardless of what the hook returned, so a hook can pass a call along but cannot force it past a matching deny rule.
distractorNotes.c: The allowed-tools list pre-approves what it names; it does not restrict anything. Unlisted tools are simply unmatched by any allow rule and fall through to the mode, where bypassPermissions approves them. Blocking specific tools under that mode requires deny entries.
distractorNotes.d: dontAsk mode turns what would have been a prompt into a denial and skips the callback entirely, which is what makes it a hard-deny posture rather than a silent one.
distractorNotes.e: Deny rules are evaluated before the mode is consulted, so a matching deny rule blocks the call even under bypassPermissions.

sourceNote: Section 'How permissions are evaluated', plus the auto-approved tools warning under 'Allow and deny rules' and the mode descriptions under 'Permission modes'
scopeNote: Hooks as a guardrail are in scope, but discrimination requires reciting the full permission evaluation order and the exact mode names bypassPermissions and dontAsk.

stem: After an agent has analysed a module across several turns, an engineer wants to explore a different design direction from that point without losing the original line of work, so they fork the session. Select TWO statements that accurately describe what forking does.

options.text: Forking also snapshots the working tree, so any file changes made inside the fork are reverted as soon as the original session is resumed from the point where it left off.
The fork begins from a copy of the original session's history and receives its own session ID, while the original session's ID and history are left unchanged.
Forking branches the conversation only, so any file changes the forked agent makes are real and visible to anything else working in that directory.
A branch is created by continuing the most recent session rather than by resuming a specific one, so the fork option applies only to the newest session.
The fork supersedes the original session, which can no longer be resumed once the branch exists and must be recreated from scratch if it is needed again.
A fork can only be created by the same process that originally created the session, since the branch point is held in memory rather than written to disk.

explanation: Forking is requested by resuming a session with the fork option set. It produces a second, independent session seeded with a copy of the original's history, and both can be resumed separately afterwards. The scope of the branch is the conversation transcript and nothing else. Because sessions persist the conversation rather than the filesystem, an agent running in the fork writes to the same working directory as any other session there, and those writes are ordinary file changes. Branching and reverting file state is a separate concern handled by file checkpointing, which is why the two features are documented as complements rather than alternatives.

distractorNotes.a: Sessions persist the conversation, not the filesystem, and forking inherits that scope. Snapshotting and restoring file state is what file checkpointing is for.
distractorNotes.d: Continuing picks up the most recent session in the directory and adds to it, which extends a single thread rather than creating a second one. A branch requires resuming a session with the fork option set.
distractorNotes.e: The original is untouched by the fork. Resuming it afterwards continues its own history, which is the entire reason to fork instead of simply continuing.
distractorNotes.f: Sessions are written to disk so they can be returned to later, including after a process restart, provided the session is reachable from the host doing the resuming.

sourceNote: Sections 'Continue, resume, and fork' and 'Fork to explore alternatives'

stem: A team builds a document analysis endpoint. Each request bundles roughly 40,000 tokens of reference material together with the analyst's question, a short instruction block, and two worked examples, all in a single user message. Quality on multi-document requests is inconsistent. Following Anthropic's long context prompting guidance, how should that message be ordered?

options.text: Place the question first so the model knows what to look for before it reads any reference material.
Repeat the question immediately after each individual document so every document is paired with the ask.
Place the reference material first, near the top, and put the question, instructions, and examples after it.
Place the reference material last, directly before the response, so the source material is the most recently read content.

explanation: Anthropic's long context guidance applies to data-rich inputs of roughly 20,000 tokens or more and is explicit about ordering: put longform data near the top of the prompt, above the query, instructions, and examples. The documentation reports that placing queries at the end improved response quality by up to 30 percent in testing, with the largest gains on complex, multi-document inputs. The effect is about where the query sits relative to the bulk of the material, so the fix here is structural rather than a matter of rewriting the instruction text. The same section adds two complementary techniques for this shape of prompt: tag each document with its source metadata, and ask for relevant quotes to be pulled out before the analysis begins.

distractorNotes.a: This inverts the documented recommendation. Leading with the question and trailing the documents is the arrangement the guidance advises against for large inputs.
distractorNotes.b: Repeating the query between documents inflates the prompt without addressing placement, and the documented benefit comes specifically from a query positioned after the full body of longform data.
distractorNotes.d: This is the opposite of the published advice. Longform data belongs at the top of the prompt, with the query at the end.

sourceNote: Long context prompting section, which covers inputs of 20k+ tokens: 'Put longform data at the top' above the query, instructions, and examples, with the note that queries at the end can improve response quality by up to 30 percent in tests on complex multidocument inputs.

stem: An engineer is assembling a prompt that mixes standing instructions, several supplied source documents, and a user question, and wants the boundaries between those parts to be unambiguous. Which TWO practices does Anthropic's prompting guidance recommend for structuring this prompt with tags? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Choose tag names from a fixed reserved vocabulary, since only a predefined set of names is recognised.
Rely on the service to parse the tags and return each tagged section back as a separate content block in the response.
Give each supplied document its own indexed tag containing separate subtags for its source metadata and for its content.
Encode the whole prompt as JSON instead, because tagged markup is not a supported way to delimit prompt sections.
Set a dedicated request header to activate tag-aware prompt parsing before tagged sections take effect.
Use consistent, descriptive tag names across prompts, and nest tags where the content has a natural hierarchy.

explanation: Tags help the model separate instructions from context, examples, and variable inputs when a prompt mixes several kinds of content. The documented best practices are to use consistent, descriptive tag names and to nest tags where the content has a genuine hierarchy, and the guidance illustrates that hierarchy with a multi-document layout in which each document sits inside its own indexed tag alongside distinct subtags for source metadata and body content. This is prompt-authoring convention rather than a request feature: the tags are ordinary text that the model reads, so there is nothing to enable, no reserved name list, and no change to the shape of the response.

distractorNotes.a: Tag names are arbitrary text chosen by the prompt author. The guidance asks only that they be descriptive and used consistently; there is no reserved list.
distractorNotes.b: Tags in the prompt do not cause the response to be segmented into corresponding content blocks. Constrained response shapes come from separate output formatting features, not from input tagging.
distractorNotes.d: This overstates the case in the opposite direction. Tagged markup is exactly what the guidance recommends for delimiting mixed prompt sections, and JSON is not required.
distractorNotes.e: No header or flag governs tagged prompt sections. They are ordinary text in the prompt and take effect immediately.

sourceNote: Structure prompts with XML tags section: use consistent, descriptive tag names and nest tags when content has a natural hierarchy, illustrated with documents nested inside an indexed document tag; the adjacent long context prompting section shows the same layout with separate source and document content subtags.

stem: A support team is adding examples to a ticket classification prompt to make the output format and label choices more consistent. Which approach best matches Anthropic's published guidance on using examples?

options.text: Include one carefully polished example, since additional examples mainly consume tokens without changing behaviour.
Enumerate every edge case the team has ever seen as its own example, so that no scenario is left unrepresented.
Omit examples and instead describe the desired output in prose at length, because examples steer tone and voice but have little bearing on the structure of the output.
Include roughly three to five examples that closely mirror real tickets and vary enough to cover edge cases, each wrapped in its own example tag.

explanation: Examples are described as one of the most reliable levers for steering output format, tone, and structure, and the guidance names three qualities to aim for: relevance, so the examples mirror the actual use case; diversity, so edge cases are covered and the model does not pick up an unintended pattern; and structure, achieved by wrapping each example in an example tag and the whole set in an enclosing tag so examples are distinguishable from instructions. The documentation gives a concrete target of three to five examples for best results, and notes that the model can be asked to assess a draft example set for relevance and diversity or to generate additional examples from an initial set.

distractorNotes.a: A single example gives the model no signal about which features of the example are essential and which are incidental. The published target is three to five, and diversity across them is part of the point.
distractorNotes.b: Exhaustive enumeration works against the diversity criterion and bloats the prompt. A small curated set that spans the space is what the guidance calls for.
distractorNotes.c: This contradicts the guidance, which presents examples as a primary tool for steering output format and structure, not merely tone.

sourceNote: Use examples effectively section: examples should be relevant, diverse, and structured by wrapping them in example tags, with the stated tip to include three to five examples for best results and the suggestion to have the model evaluate or extend an example set.

stem: A developer wants every response from an internal assistant to be framed as coming from a specialist in a narrow technical area, so that tone and focus stay consistent across a multi-turn conversation. What is the documented way to establish this role in a Messages API request?

options.text: Set the request's top-level system field to a short description of the role.
Insert an entry with a system role as the first item in the messages array.
Begin the reply on the developer's behalf by supplying a partial assistant turn that states the persona.
Restate the role at the start of every user message, because role framing does not carry across turns.

explanation: The role is set through the request's dedicated top-level system field, which sits alongside model, max_tokens, and messages rather than inside the messages list. The documentation notes that even a single sentence of role framing focuses behaviour and tone for a use case, and its examples across every SDK pass the role string to that field. Because system content is sent with each request, the framing already applies to every turn without being repeated in user messages.

distractorNotes.b: The Messages API carries system content in its own top-level field; entries in the messages array use the user and assistant roles.
distractorNotes.c: Supplying a partial assistant turn to steer the reply is a legacy technique that current guidance directs developers away from, and it was never the documented mechanism for setting a role.
distractorNotes.d: System content is sent with every request, so the framing already applies to each turn. Repeating it in user messages adds tokens without adding effect.

sourceNote: Give Claude a role section: setting a role in the system prompt focuses behaviour and tone, and even a single sentence makes a difference; the SDK examples all pass the role string to the request's top-level system field.

stem: An agent is hitting its context limit sooner than its developer expected, and the developer is auditing what actually consumes the window. Which THREE statements about context window accounting are correct? (Select THREE.)

options.text: The system prompt is handled separately from the conversation and is excluded from the window.
Only input counts toward the window; the tokens the model generates for the turn fall outside it.
The tool definitions supplied with a request consume window space, whether or not a tool is called on that turn.
Tool results, images, and documents carried inside the messages array consume window space like any other input.
Of the token fields reported in usage, only the plain input token count applies to the window, because the cache-related counts are billing metrics that sit outside it.
Tokens served from the prompt cache still occupy the window; caching changes what those tokens cost, not whether they count.

explanation: The context window covers everything in the request plus what the model produces for that turn. That explicitly includes the system prompt, every message in the messages array along with tool results, images, and documents, and the tool definitions themselves, which is why the documentation points developers at separate techniques for reducing tool-definition overhead. Prompt caching is a frequent source of confusion: the cache read and cache creation counts reported in usage all count toward the window, so caching reduces what those tokens cost without freeing any space. Because the window is finite and recall degrades as it fills, the documentation frames curating what occupies it as being as important as how much room is available, and points to the token counting API for estimating a request before it is sent.

distractorNotes.a: The system prompt is counted along with everything else in the request. There is no separate allowance for it.
distractorNotes.b: Output is part of the window, and it also becomes input on the following turn, so a window must accommodate the response as well as the prompt.
distractorNotes.e: All three token fields reported in usage count toward the window. Treating cached tokens as free space is the specific misconception the documentation warns about.

sourceNote: How the context window works section: everything in the request counts, including the system prompt, every message with its tool results, images, and documents, and the tool definitions, plus the generated output; the input count splits across input, cache read, and cache creation tokens and all three count, and cached prefixes still occupy the window because caching changes what you pay rather than whether tokens count.

stem: A team enables server-side tool result clearing on a long-running agent that accumulates large file reads and search results. During review, someone asks how the application's own stored conversation history should be maintained now that older tool results are being cleared. What is correct?

options.text: The application must apply the same clearing to its local history, or subsequent requests will be rejected as inconsistent.
The response carries an edited transcript that the application is expected to store in place of its previous history.
The application keeps its full, unmodified history and keeps sending it; the clearing is applied server-side before the prompt reaches the model.
Clearing permanently removes the affected tool results from the conversation, so the application should archive them elsewhere first if it may need them.

explanation: Context editing is applied server-side, before the prompt reaches the model, and the documentation states directly that the client keeps the full unmodified conversation history and does not need to sync its state with the edited version. When the configured threshold is exceeded, the oldest tool results are cleared in chronological order and each is replaced with placeholder text signalling to the model that content was removed; by default only the results are cleared, with an option to clear the tool call inputs as well. Because the edit is recomputed per request against whatever history is sent, the client-side record remains the durable source of truth and is unaffected. A practical consequence worth knowing is that clearing tool results invalidates cached prompt prefixes, so a minimum-clearing threshold is provided to make each invalidation worth the cache write.

distractorNotes.a: No client-side mirroring is required or expected. The documentation calls out explicitly that you continue managing your full history locally as normal.
distractorNotes.b: The response does not return an edited transcript for the client to adopt. The edit is applied to the prompt on the way in, not handed back as replacement state.
distractorNotes.d: Nothing is removed from the application's own records, so there is nothing to archive defensively. Clearing affects only what the model sees for a given request.

sourceNote: Context editing happens server-side section: edits are applied before the prompt reaches the model, the client maintains the full unmodified history, and no client state sync is needed; the tool result clearing and prompt caching sections describe oldest-first clearing with placeholder replacement text, the optional clearing of tool inputs, and cache invalidation with a minimum-clearing parameter.

stem: A developer is configuring server-side compaction for a long-running assistant, wants summaries that emphasise code snippets and technical decisions, and wants compaction to trigger earlier than the default. Which TWO statements about configuring compaction are correct? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Custom instructions are appended to the default summarization prompt, so default behaviours such as recording remaining next steps are retained automatically.
The trigger can alternatively be expressed as a number of conversation turns or an elapsed wall-clock duration.
Compaction is performed in the client SDK, so the application must generate the summary and resend a shortened history itself.
Supplying custom summarization instructions replaces the default summarization prompt entirely rather than adding to it.
The trigger is expressed as an input token threshold, and the documented minimum value that may be configured is fifty thousand tokens.
After a summary is produced, the application must strip the superseded earlier content blocks before issuing the next request.

explanation: Compaction summarizes older conversation content automatically as the input approaches a configured threshold, and two configuration details are easy to get wrong. First, custom instructions completely replace the default summarization prompt, so anything the default did that still matters, such as recording current state and next steps for a future context window, has to be restated in the custom text. Second, the trigger accepts only an input token type, with a documented default of one hundred fifty thousand tokens and a documented minimum of fifty thousand, so lowering the threshold is the supported way to compact earlier. Operationally the summary arrives as a compaction block in the response; the application appends that response to its messages and content preceding the block is dropped automatically on later requests. An option is available to pause once the summary has been generated so that additional content can be inserted before the response continues.

distractorNotes.a: The documentation states that custom instructions do not supplement the default prompt but replace it completely. Assuming the default behaviours survive is the trap this option sets.
distractorNotes.b: Input tokens is the only supported trigger type. Turn counts and elapsed time are not configurable trigger dimensions.
distractorNotes.c: This describes a client-side summarization approach. The compaction being configured here runs server-side, which is why it is recommended over hand-rolled summarization code.
distractorNotes.f: Content preceding the compaction block is dropped automatically once the response containing that block is appended, so manual stripping is not part of the flow.

sourceNote: Parameters table and Custom summarization instructions section: input tokens is the only supported trigger type with a default of 150,000 and a stated minimum of 50,000, and custom instructions completely replace the default prompt when provided; the How compaction works and Pausing after compaction sections cover the compaction block, automatic dropping of prior blocks, and the pause option.
scopeNote: Compaction is a legitimate context-engineering topic, but one correct option turns on recalling the documented 50,000-token minimum trigger value.

stem: A compliance tool sends user-supplied documents with citations enabled so that each claim can be traced back to a source passage. A developer then adds a JSON schema output format to the same request so the answer can be parsed directly into a typed record. What is the result?

options.text: The request succeeds, but citations are silently ignored and the response contains only the schema-conforming JSON.
The request fails with a client error, because citations and schema-constrained JSON output cannot be combined.
The request succeeds, and the citation details are folded into the JSON as an additional property alongside the schema fields.
The request succeeds only if the documents are PDFs, since page-level citations can be represented inside a JSON schema.

explanation: The two features are documented as mutually exclusive. Enabling citations on any user-supplied document block while also specifying an output format returns a 400 error rather than degrading gracefully. The reason is mechanical: citations work by interleaving citation blocks with text blocks in the response so that each claim travels with the passages supporting it, whereas schema-constrained JSON output forces the entire response to conform to a single schema. Those two response shapes cannot coexist. An application that needs both traceability and typed data has to separate the concerns, for example by obtaining the cited response first and performing extraction as a distinct call.

distractorNotes.a: The documented behaviour is an explicit error, not a silent downgrade. Nothing is quietly dropped.
distractorNotes.c: There is no merged representation. Citations are delivered as separate blocks interleaved with text, which is precisely what the schema constraint precludes.
distractorNotes.d: Document type is irrelevant to the conflict. The incompatibility concerns the structure of the response, not any particular citation index format.

sourceNote: Feature compatibility section: the warning that citations and structured outputs are incompatible, with a 400 error returned when citations are enabled on a user-provided document or search result block and an output format parameter is also supplied, because citations require interleaving citation blocks with text output.
scopeNote: Structured output is a named Output Handling topic, but the item tests one specific feature-interaction rule, that citations and schema-constrained output cannot be combined.

stem: A knowledge base assistant attaches several documents per request with citations enabled, and the team is reviewing cost and behaviour before rollout. Which TWO statements about the citations feature are correct? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Enabling citations slightly increases input tokens, but the cited text returned with each citation does not count toward output tokens.
Citations can be enabled on the subset of documents considered authoritative, leaving the remaining documents attached to the request but uncited.
Regions of images embedded in a PDF can be cited in the same way as text extracted from that PDF, using the same citation blocks on the response.
Plain text and PDF documents both return citations as zero-indexed character offsets into the source, which keeps client-side handling uniform.
A document's title and context fields are passed to the model but cannot be cited from, which makes context a suitable place for metadata.
Enabling citations reduces input tokens, because the model no longer needs to restate source passages in its reasoning or repeat them in its answer text.

explanation: Two properties matter for planning. On cost, enabling citations adds a small amount of input overhead from added system content and document chunking, while the cited text accompanying each citation is excluded from output token counts and is also excluded from input counts when passed back on later turns; this is one of the documented advantages over simply prompting the model to quote its sources. On document shape, only the source content is citable, whereas the title and context fields are passed to the model without ever appearing as cited content, and because title is length-limited the context field is the recommended home for metadata as text or stringified JSON. Two further constraints are worth remembering: citations must currently be enabled on all documents in a request or on none of them, and only text citations are supported.

distractorNotes.b: Citations are all or nothing within a request. Mixing cited and uncited documents in one request is not supported.
distractorNotes.c: Only text citations are supported, and citing images from PDFs is specifically called out as not currently possible.
distractorNotes.d: The index format varies by document type. Plain text uses zero-indexed character ranges, PDFs use one-indexed page numbers, and custom content uses zero-indexed block indices.
distractorNotes.f: This reverses the documented cost profile. Input tokens rise slightly, and the savings appear on the output side.

sourceNote: How citations work, Citable versus non-citable content, Citation indices, and Token costs sections: citations must be enabled on all or none of the documents in a request and only text citations are supported; title and context are passed to the model but not cited from; index formats differ by document type; enabling citations slightly increases input tokens while cited text counts toward neither output tokens nor input tokens on replay.
scopeNote: Turns on fine-grained citations accounting, including that cited text is excluded from output tokens and that title and context fields cannot be cited from.

stem: A developer is deciding how much execution plumbing their service needs to build. Which statement correctly describes the division of responsibility between client tools and server tools in the Claude API?

options.text: Both kinds run on Anthropic's infrastructure, and the label records only whether the developer or Anthropic authored the tool's schema rather than where the code behind it actually executes when Claude calls it in a request.
Client tools are restricted to the schemas Anthropic publishes, such as bash and the text editor; any tool the developer defines is by definition a server tool that Anthropic executes on request.

Server tools behave exactly like client tools in the message loop: the application receives each call and must return a matching tool_result block before the conversation can continue to the next turn.

Client tools run inside the developer's application, which returns the outcome in a tool_result block to continue the exchange; server tools run on Anthropic's infrastructure and the application never executes them.

explanation: The client and server split is about where the code runs. For a client tool, Claude emits a tool_use block, the application performs the work, and the outcome travels back in a tool_result block. For a server tool, Anthropic runs the operation and the results appear in the response without the application executing anything or returning a result block. Both kinds are declared in the same tools array of the request, so the execution boundary, rather than where the tool is declared, is the thing to reason about when planning what to build.

distractorNotes.a: Authorship of the schema is not the dividing line. Anthropic publishes schemas for several client tools, and those still execute in the developer's environment, so schema origin and execution location vary independently.
distractorNotes.b: This inverts the categories. User-defined tools are client tools, and Anthropic-schema tools such as the bash and text editor tools are also client tools, because the developer's application performs the work in both cases.
distractorNotes.c: Server tool calls are resolved by Anthropic within the request. Returning tool_result blocks for them is not part of the flow, and treating them like client tools leads developers to build handling that will never be invoked.

sourceNote: Tool use with Claude — 'How tool use works'

stem: An internal assistant exposes a tool named lookup_account whose entire description reads "Gets account data." In testing, Claude often calls a neighbouring reporting tool instead, or calls lookup_account with parameters that make no sense for the request. According to Anthropic's tool design guidance, which change has the largest effect on tool selection performance?

options.text: Break the tool apart into a family of single-purpose tools so that each one covers exactly one action and its name alone makes the right choice obvious to the model.
Rewrite the description into several sentences stating what the tool does, when it should and should not be used, what each parameter controls, and what the tool does not return.
Leave the description as it is and move all of the explanatory detail about the tool, including when to prefer it over the neighbouring reporting tool, into the shared system prompt instead.
Force the tool to be used on every turn so that the model no longer has to choose between the available tools and always produces a call the application can handle.

explanation: Anthropic's guidance is explicit that the description is by far the strongest lever on tool performance, and it recommends aiming for at least three or four sentences, more for a complex tool. A strong description covers behaviour, the conditions under which the tool applies, the meaning and effect of each parameter, and caveats such as information the tool deliberately omits. The failure described here is a selection and argument-construction failure, which is precisely what a thorough description addresses.

distractorNotes.a: The published guidance points the other way: it recommends consolidating related operations into fewer, more capable tools, often behind an action parameter, because a sprawling surface of near-identical tools increases selection ambiguity rather than reducing it.
distractorNotes.c: The tool description is the context attached to the tool itself and is what the model weighs when choosing among tools. Relocating that detail into the system prompt leaves the decision point under-specified and wastes the field designed to carry it.
distractorNotes.d: Forcing tool use guarantees that a call happens, but it does nothing to make the arguments correct or the choice appropriate, and it suppresses the model's ability to answer without a tool when that is the right outcome.

sourceNote: Define tools — 'Best practices for tool definitions'

stem: A team keeps receiving errors reporting that tool_use identifiers were found without tool_result blocks immediately after them. Select THREE statements that describe the required construction of a message carrying tool results.

options.text: The results belong in the user message that comes immediately after the assistant turn containing the tool_use blocks, with no other message placed in between.
Tool results are supplied under a dedicated tool role rather than the user role, so that they remain clearly separate from ordinary conversation turns in the stored transcript.
Each tool_result block must be delivered in its own separate user message so results can be attributed unambiguously.
Within that message's content array, every tool_result block must appear before any text block.
The content field is mandatory on every tool_result block, so a tool that produces no output must be given a placeholder value.
Each result is bound to the call it answers by the tool_use_id field, which repeats the identifier from the corresponding tool_use block.

explanation: The Claude API folds tool interaction into the ordinary user and assistant message structure rather than introducing a special role. Results must follow their calls immediately in the history, must lead the content array ahead of any text, and are matched to their calls through tool_use_id. Placing text ahead of the results is a documented cause of a 400 response, and the immediacy requirement is what the error about missing result blocks is reporting.

distractorNotes.b: There is no tool role in this API. Tool results are carried in user messages and tool calls in assistant messages, which is a noted difference from APIs that introduce a separate role for function output.
distractorNotes.c: Splitting results across messages breaks the immediacy requirement for every call after the first. All results answering a single assistant turn belong together in one user message.
distractorNotes.e: The content field is optional. A tool_result block carrying only a tool_use_id is valid, so inventing placeholder content is unnecessary and can mislead the model about what the tool returned.

sourceNote: Handle tool calls — 'Handling results from client tools', including the 'Important formatting requirements' note

stem: A client tool that queries an internal pricing service times out after Claude calls it. The developer wants the assistant to recover gracefully and, where possible, adapt rather than stall. What is the documented way to continue the conversation?

options.text: Omit the tool_result block for the failed call so that Claude notices the gap in the exchange and reissues the request on the next turn without being told what went wrong.
Skip the result block and instead send a plain user text message explaining that the pricing service is unavailable and stating what Claude should do next.
Return a tool_result block for that call with is_error set to true and content stating what failed and what Claude should do next, such as how long to wait before retrying.
Remove the failing tool from the tools array on the follow-up request so Claude cannot attempt it again, and let it answer from what it already has in context.

explanation: Failures are reported through the same result channel as successes: a tool_result block with is_error set to true. Claude then incorporates the failure into its reply, and the guidance is to write instructive error text rather than a bare failure token, because that message is the only context Claude has for deciding whether to retry, choose a different approach, or explain the limitation to the user. The same pattern covers calls the application deliberately declines to run.

distractorNotes.a: A missing result leaves the tool call unanswered, which violates the requirement that results follow their calls immediately and produces a request error rather than a retry.
distractorNotes.b: Text in place of a result does not resolve the outstanding tool call. Text may accompany results in the same message, but only after every result block, and it cannot substitute for one.
distractorNotes.d: Withdrawing the tool changes the available surface mid-conversation without answering the outstanding call, and it removes the option of a legitimate retry once the service recovers.

sourceNote: Handle tool calls — 'Handling errors with is_error', 'Tool execution error'

stem: An agent turn returns three tool_use blocks at once: two read-only lookups and one write that must not run if a lookup fails. Select THREE statements that correctly describe how parallel tool calls work and where the developer's responsibility lies.

options.text: The API runs the calls concurrently on the application's behalf and delivers a single merged result for the turn.
A single assistant turn can contain several tool_use blocks, and the application decides whether to run them concurrently, in sequence, or in some combination.
Every call from that turn is answered with its own tool_result block, and all of those blocks are returned together in the next single user message.
If the application chooses not to run one of the calls, it still returns a tool_result for it, marked as an error and explaining why it was skipped.
Results must be returned in separate user messages, one per call, ordered to match the order in which the calls appeared.
Emitting more than one tool_use block in a single turn is opt-in and must be switched on with a request parameter before Claude will produce parallel calls in a response at all.

explanation: Parallel tool use is on by default, and the API deliberately does not prescribe an execution order, leaving the strategy to the application. Independent read-only work is usually safe to run concurrently for lower latency, while calls with side effects, shared state, or ordering requirements are often better run in sequence. Whatever strategy is chosen, the message contract is unchanged: one result per call, all in the next user message, each matched by tool_use_id and placed ahead of any text. A call that is deliberately skipped still needs a result block flagged as an error so that no call is left unanswered.

distractorNotes.a: Execution of client tools never happens inside the API. The response describes what Claude wants to call; scheduling, concurrency, and error handling are entirely the application's to implement.
distractorNotes.e: One message per result breaks the requirement that results immediately follow their calls, and it is precisely the pattern that stops parallel behaviour from working correctly on later turns.
distractorNotes.f: Multiple calls per turn are the default behaviour. The available parameter works in the opposite direction, constraining Claude to fewer calls rather than enabling more.

sourceNote: Parallel tool use — 'Execution semantics'

stem: A regulated workflow steps through one audited action at a time on a model that supports forced tool use. Each assistant turn must produce exactly one tool call: never two, and never a turn that answers in prose without calling anything. Which request configuration meets that requirement?

options.text: Set tool_choice to type any and set disable_parallel_tool_use to true.
Set tool_choice to type auto and set disable_parallel_tool_use to true.
Set tool_choice to type any and leave disable_parallel_tool_use unset.
Set tool_choice to type none and set disable_parallel_tool_use to true.

explanation: Two independent controls combine here. The tool_choice type governs whether a tool must be called at all: any obliges Claude to call one of the supplied tools, while auto leaves it free to answer in text. The disable_parallel_tool_use flag governs how many calls a turn may contain. Under any or tool, that flag yields exactly one call; under auto it yields at most one, which still permits a turn with no call. Only a forcing tool_choice combined with the flag produces the exactly-one guarantee, and forcing types are available on models that support forced tool use.

distractorNotes.b: Under auto the flag caps the turn at one call but does not compel a call, so Claude may still reply in plain text and produce a turn containing zero tool calls.
distractorNotes.c: Forcing a tool without the flag guarantees at least one call but places no ceiling on the number, so a turn may contain several calls and break the one-action-at-a-time requirement.
distractorNotes.d: The none type prevents tool use altogether, which is the opposite of the requirement and makes the parallel setting irrelevant.

sourceNote: Parallel tool use — 'Exactly one tool call', read with 'Define tools' on the four tool_choice options
scopeNote: Every option is a permutation of exact parameter values for tool_choice and disable_parallel_tool_use. Discrimination is entirely at the parameter level.

stem: A booking agent keeps receiving a passenger count as a string rather than an integer, and occasionally a required field is missing entirely. A colleague suggests enabling strict tool use. Select TWO statements that are accurate about strict tool use.

options.text: The value the tool returns is validated against a schema before Claude is allowed to read it.
The input object in a tool_use block conforms to the declared input schema, so mistyped values and absent required fields stop occurring.
The underlying operation is guaranteed to succeed at runtime once the call has been made.
The tool name in a tool_use block is always a valid name drawn from the tools made available for the request.
It can be switched on for a Model Context Protocol toolset entry, which enforces the same input validation across every tool that the server exposes to the request.

explanation: Strict tool use constrains token sampling to outputs the schema permits, a technique known as grammar-constrained sampling. The resulting guarantees are narrow and precise: the tool input conforms to the schema, and the tool name is always one that genuinely exists. That removes the class of failures described here without any validate-and-retry loop of the developer's own. It says nothing about what happens once the developer's code runs, and it is not accepted on every kind of entry in the tools array.

distractorNotes.a: Strict mode acts on what the model generates, which is the tool call. Whatever a tool returns is produced by the developer's own code and is not schema-checked by this feature.
distractorNotes.c: Well-formed arguments are not the same as a successful operation. A call with perfect inputs can still fail on a network timeout or a rejected business rule, which is why error results remain necessary.
distractorNotes.e: Strict mode is not among the properties available on a Model Context Protocol toolset entry. Restricting or shaping which of a server's tools are exposed is done through that toolset's own configuration instead.

sourceNote: Strict tool use — the 'Guarantees' list following the 'Quick start' samples and 'How it works', read with 'Tool reference' — 'Tool definition properties' for where strict is unavailable

stem: A team packages an internal catalogue service as a Model Context Protocol server. Engineers run one copy as a process on their own machines alongside the AI application, and the platform team runs a hosted copy that many users reach over the network. Which statement matches the protocol's architecture?

options.text: The host creates one client per server connection, and the process on an engineer's machine is reached over the stdio transport while the hosted copy is reached over streamable HTTP.
The host maintains a single client that multiplexes traffic to every server it uses, so adding a second server reuses the existing connection rather than opening another one.

Servers initiate the connection to the host and register the capabilities they offer, which is why one hosted server can reach many hosts at once without any per-host configuration on the client side.
The stdio transport can serve clients across the network as well as on the same machine, so the choice of transport is independent of where the server process actually runs.

explanation: The protocol follows a client-server shape in which the host is the AI application, and the host instantiates a dedicated client for each server it connects to, so a host talking to three servers holds three clients and three connections. The two transports map onto deployment: stdio uses standard input and output streams for direct communication between processes on the same machine, while streamable HTTP carries messages over the network and is what remote deployments use. The words local and remote describe where a server runs, not a difference in what a server fundamentally is.

distractorNotes.b: Each client maintains its own dedicated connection to a single server. Connecting to an additional server causes the host to instantiate an additional client rather than reuse an existing one.
distractorNotes.c: The direction is reversed. The host, through its clients, establishes connections to servers; servers do not reach out to register themselves with hosts.
distractorNotes.d: The stdio transport is for direct process communication on the same machine and carries no network overhead precisely because there is no network hop. Reaching a server across the network requires the HTTP-based transport.

sourceNote: Architecture overview — 'Participants' and 'Transport layer'

stem: An architect plans to attach a partner's Model Context Protocol server to a service through the Messages API connector, without building a protocol client. Select THREE statements that correctly describe the constraints and responsibilities of that approach.

options.text: The server has to be reachable at a publicly exposed HTTPS URL; a server that speaks only over standard input and output on a developer's machine cannot be attached directly.
Only tool calls are available through the connector, so other capabilities a server might expose, such as resources and prompt templates, are out of scope.
A single server definition may be referenced by several toolset entries, which is the supported way to expose different subsets of that server's tools within a single request to the Messages API.
Naming a tool in the per-tool configuration that the server does not actually expose causes the request to fail validation.
The calling application obtains the access token for an authenticated server and refreshes it as needed, passing it in the server definition.
Enabling strict schema validation on the toolset entry applies that guarantee to every tool the server exposes.

explanation: The connector removes the need to implement a protocol client, but it narrows what is available in exchange. Servers are declared by URL and must be publicly reachable over HTTPS, which rules out attaching a purely local process directly; only the tool-calling portion of the protocol is surfaced; and the authorisation flow stays with the caller, which obtains and refreshes the token itself. Teams that need local servers or the capabilities the connector omits are pointed instead toward managing their own protocol client connection, for which the SDKs provide client-side helper functions.

distractorNotes.c: Each server must be referenced by exactly one toolset entry, and each toolset entry maps to one server. Differentiating which tools are exposed is done inside that single entry through its default and per-tool configuration.
distractorNotes.d: An unrecognised tool name in the per-tool configuration is tolerated: a warning is recorded and the request proceeds, deliberately, because a server's set of tools can change over time.
distractorNotes.f: Strict schema validation is not among the properties accepted on a Model Context Protocol toolset entry. Control over that server's tools is exercised by enabling or disabling them and by deferring their loading.

sourceNote: MCP connector — 'Limitations', 'Validation rules', and 'Authentication'

stem: A support application asks Claude to summarize inbound emails from unknown senders. The team wants Claude to treat every email body as data rather than as instructions it might follow. Following Anthropic's guidance on indirect prompt injection, where should the retrieved email body be placed in the request?

options.text: Appended to the system prompt inside XML tags labelled as untrusted, so that the handling policy and the content it governs stay together in one place
Inside a tool_result block, with the tool description stating that the content is the body of an inbound email from an unknown sender
In a plain user text block introduced by a sentence telling Claude to ignore any instructions that appear in the text that follows it
Split across several consecutive user turns so that no single turn contains a complete instruction that the model could act on

explanation: Anthropic's guidance is to deliver third-party content to Claude inside tool_result blocks and never in system prompts or plain user text blocks, because Claude is trained to treat instructions appearing inside tool results with appropriate skepticism. The guidance also asks you to make the nature and source of the content explicit, either in the tool description or in the structure of the result, so Claude can calibrate how much to trust any directives embedded in it. Encoding the payload as a JSON string strengthens this further, since JSON escaping gives unambiguous delimiters that an attacker cannot close in order to break out into an instruction context.

distractorNotes.a: The guidance does place an untrusted-content policy in the system prompt, but never the untrusted content itself. Content sitting in the system prompt inherits the authority of your own instructions, which is the trust level an injection is trying to reach.
distractorNotes.c: A plain user text block is the other placement the guidance rules out. A preamble telling Claude to disregard what follows is a prompt-level hint rather than a structural signal, and it leaves the untrusted text in a trusted position.
distractorNotes.d: Fragmenting the content does not change its trust level. The control that matters is which block type carries the content, not how many turns it spans, and splitting it also degrades the summary.

sourceNote: Section "Indirect prompt injection", bullets "Put untrusted content only in tool results" (deliver third-party content inside tool_result blocks, never in system prompts or plain user text blocks), "Tell Claude what the content is and where it came from", and "State the policy in your system prompt".

stem: An agent retrieves web pages and documents on a trusted user's behalf, so the adversary controls the retrieved content rather than the user's prompt. Which THREE practices does Anthropic's guidance recommend for limiting the damage an embedded instruction can do? Select THREE.

options.text: Encode third-party strings as JSON so that escaping provides unambiguous delimiters around the untrusted payload
Screen each tool's raw output with a lightweight classifier call constrained by structured outputs, and return the content only when the screen reports no injection attempt
Place your own operating instructions inside the tool_result block so that they sit directly next to the untrusted content they are meant to govern and cannot be separated from it later
Apply least privilege by withholding secrets the agent does not need, running tools in sandboxed environments, and scoping permissions narrowly
Raise the sampling temperature so that Claude is less likely to reproduce an embedded instruction verbatim
Rely on the model's inherent resistance to injection instead of adding application-level controls

explanation: The recommended defenses are layered. JSON encoding wraps the untrusted string so an attacker cannot close a quote or tag and escape into an instruction context. Output screening applies the same lightweight-model pattern used for user input to the content tools return, with structured outputs making the verdict a parseable value the application can branch on before the content is handed back as a tool result. Least privilege limits the blast radius of any injection that does succeed, which is why the guidance pairs it with sandboxed execution and narrowly scoped permissions. Red-teaming the workflow with deliberately poisoned documents and continuous monitoring of outputs complete the picture.

distractorNotes.c: The guidance says the opposite: because Claude treats tool-result content as untrusted data, instructions you place there may be ignored or flagged as a possible injection. Send them in a user turn that follows the tool result instead.
distractorNotes.e: Temperature is a sampling parameter and has no bearing on whether Claude treats retrieved text as data or as a directive. It appears nowhere in the injection guidance.
distractorNotes.f: Model resistance is described as a starting point, not a substitute for guardrails. The guidance exists to add application-level layers on top of it, and the sandboxing documentation makes the same defense-in-depth argument.

sourceNote: Section "Indirect prompt injection", bullets "JSON-encode untrusted content", "Screen tool outputs before Claude acts on them" (classifier call constrained with structured outputs), "Limit Claude's access to sensitive data and actions", "Don't put your own instructions in tool results", and "Red-team your own agent".

stem: A repository's Claude Code settings contain both a deny rule for Bash(aws *) and an allow rule for Bash(aws s3 ls). During a session Claude proposes running aws s3 ls. What happens, and why?

options.text: The call runs, because the narrower allow rule is a more specific match than the broad deny rule and specificity decides which rule applies
The user is prompted to approve or reject the call, because two rules match it and the conflict between them is resolved interactively at the point where it is proposed
The call is blocked, because rules are evaluated deny, then ask, then allow, and the first match decides the outcome regardless of how specific each rule is
The outcome depends on which settings file each rule came from, with the more locally scoped file winning over the shared repository configuration

explanation: Permission rules are evaluated in a fixed order: deny, then ask, then allow. The first match in that order determines the result, and rule specificity does not change the order. A broad deny rule therefore cannot carry allowlist exceptions; to permit one command from a family you have to narrow the deny rule itself rather than add a more specific allow. The same precedence governs ask against allow, so a matching ask rule still prompts even when a narrower allow rule also matches the call. Deny rules apply in every permission mode, which is what makes them a dependable control rather than a default that a mode can relax.

distractorNotes.a: Specificity is a familiar intuition from firewall and IAM systems, but it is explicitly not how these rules are ordered. The documentation uses this exact pairing of a broad deny with a narrower allow as the example where the deny still wins.
distractorNotes.b: Prompting is what an ask rule produces, not a fallback for resolving conflicts. A matched deny rule blocks the call outright and offers no approval option.
distractorNotes.d: Settings precedence governs which rules are in effect and how they merge across scopes. Once the rules are resolved, the deny-ask-allow ordering decides the outcome, not the file a rule came from.

sourceNote: Section "Manage permissions": rules are evaluated in the order deny, ask, allow; the first match determines the outcome and rule specificity does not change the order, with Bash(aws *) against Bash(aws s3 ls) given as the worked example of a deny rule that cannot carry allowlist exceptions. That deny rules apply in every mode is stated in "Permission modes" on https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes.

stem: A team writes in its CLAUDE.md that Claude must never run the project's deployment script. A reviewer asks whether that instruction on its own prevents the tool call from executing. Which assessment is correct?

options.text: It does prevent it, because CLAUDE.md is loaded as a system-level instruction that the permission layer consults before approving any tool call proposed during the session, alongside the deny rules
It does prevent it, provided the same instruction is repeated in the first user message of every session so the model sees it before it proposes any tool call
It does not prevent it, and the only supported remedy is to run the session inside a container with no network access and no write access to the repository
It does not prevent it; what Claude Code allows is decided outside the model, so the block has to be expressed as a deny rule, a permission mode, or a PreToolUse hook

explanation: Permission rules are enforced by Claude Code itself, not by the model. Instructions in a prompt or in CLAUDE.md shape what Claude tries to do, but they do not change what the tooling allows, so a documented prohibition is guidance rather than a control. To actually grant or revoke access you use the permissions dialog, a permission rule, a permission mode, or a PreToolUse hook, each of which sits outside the model and evaluates the call before it runs. Keeping this separation clear between what steers the model and what gates the tool is the central idea in the Claude Code security model.

distractorNotes.a: CLAUDE.md is context supplied to the model, not policy consumed by the permission layer. Nothing in the permission evaluation path reads it.
distractorNotes.b: Repeating an instruction may raise the chance the model follows it but adds no enforcement. A restriction that depends on the model choosing to comply is not a control.
distractorNotes.c: The first half is right and the second is overstated. A deny rule, a permission mode, or a PreToolUse hook blocks the call directly; container isolation is a separate, coarser layer for limiting damage if something does run.

sourceNote: Note in section "Manage permissions": permission rules are enforced by Claude Code, not by the model; instructions in your prompt or CLAUDE.md shape what Claude tries to do but do not change what Claude Code allows, and access is granted or revoked with /permissions, a permission rule, a permission mode, or a PreToolUse hook.

stem: A team enables the built-in sandboxed Bash tool and asks its security reviewer what that sandbox does not protect against. Which TWO statements are accurate? Select TWO.
