Keep the work in one request and separate the draft, review, and refine stages with tags, because splitting the task into separate calls discards everything produced in the earlier stages and forces a restart from scratch.

Chain the work, because chaining is what gives you an inspectable intermediate output and a defined pipeline; the documented shape is draft, then review against explicit criteria, then refine, each step its own call.

Chain the work mainly to reduce cost, because several short requests process fewer total tokens than one longer request that has to carry the draft and the rubric through to the end of a single response.

explanation: Current guidance is that much multistep reasoning is handled inside a single response, so chaining is no longer the default answer to task complexity. What chaining still buys you is control at the seams: it is called out as useful specifically when you need to inspect intermediate outputs or enforce a particular pipeline structure. The documented canonical pattern is self-correction, meaning generate a draft, review it against criteria, then refine based on that review, with each step issued as a separate API call so the run can be logged, evaluated, or branched at any point. That is exactly the requirement here, since the rubric check must be a distinct auditable stage and the original draft has to remain visible.

distractorNotes.a: This overstates the need for chaining. Multistep reasoning is largely handled within a single response, which is why the guidance now frames chaining as a control and observability technique rather than a capability workaround.
distractorNotes.b: Separate calls do not discard earlier work; the draft and the review are passed forward as input to the next call. Keeping everything in one request is what removes the inspection point the team needs.
distractorNotes.d: Cost is not a documented rationale for chaining. Splitting a task does not inherently reduce the total tokens processed, since each call still has to carry the context it needs, and the stated reasons to chain are inspection of intermediate outputs and pipeline control.

sourceNote: Chain complex prompts section: explicit prompt chaining remains useful when you need to inspect intermediate outputs or enforce a specific pipeline structure, and the most common chaining pattern is self-correction, generating a draft, reviewing it against criteria, then refining, with each step as a separate API call so you can log, evaluate, or branch.

stem: A developer defines a JSON schema for an extraction endpoint. It marks several properties as required, sets a minimum value of 100 on a numeric field, and sets a maximum length on a string field. The schema is supplied through one of the official SDK structured-output helpers rather than by hand-building the raw request. Which TWO statements describe how this behaves? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The minimum of 100 is enforced during decoding in the same way as the declared required fields and types, so the model is structurally unable to emit a smaller number for that field.

The stripped constraints are still enforced remotely before the response is returned, because the helper registers the developer's original schema with the request, so validating the response again in application code is redundant work.

The numeric minimum and the string maximum length are stripped from the schema that is sent and surfaced in the field descriptions instead, so the response still has to be validated against the original schema in application code.

Objects remain open to extra properties unless the developer sets the additional properties flag by hand, because the helpers pass object definitions through untouched even while they strip unsupported keywords.

Within the supported subset of the schema language the response is constrained during decoding to be valid JSON with the declared required fields and types, so retry logic for parse failures is not needed.

Constraining the response to a JSON schema and requesting strict schema validation on tool inputs are mutually exclusive, so a single request may use one or the other but not both, and asking for both is rejected.

explanation: Structured outputs support only a subset of the JSON Schema language, and the official SDK helpers bridge that gap by transforming the schema before it is sent. The documented steps are to remove unsupported constraints such as minimum, maximum, minimum length and maximum length, to fold that information into the property description so the model still sees the intent as guidance, to add the additional properties flag set to false on every object, to filter string formats down to the supported list, and then to validate the returned response against the developer's original schema including all constraints. The practical takeaway is that the model receives a simplified schema while the application still enforces the full one, so range and length rules are guidance plus a client-side check rather than a decoding guarantee. What constrained decoding does guarantee is the structural part: valid parseable JSON with the declared required fields and types, which is why the documentation says schema violations no longer require retries.

distractorNotes.a: Value range constraints are among the unsupported keywords that are removed before the schema is sent. The minimum survives only as descriptive guidance and as a client-side validation check, not as a decoding constraint.
distractorNotes.b: Nothing enforces the stripped constraints remotely, because they are removed before the schema is sent. That is exactly why the transformation ends with a client-side validation step against the developer's original schema.
distractorNotes.d: The SDKs explicitly do modify the schema, and adding the additional properties flag set to false on all objects is one of the documented transformation steps.
distractorNotes.f: Schema-constrained JSON output and strict schema validation on tool inputs are described as two complementary features that may be used independently or together in the same request.

sourceNote: How SDK transformation works subsection: the SDK helpers remove unsupported constraints such as minimum, maximum, minimum length and maximum length, move the constraint info into the description, add additional properties false to all objects, filter string formats, and validate responses against the original schema, so the model receives a simplified schema while application code still enforces all constraints; the Why use structured outputs section states that constrained decoding yields always-valid, type-safe output with guaranteed required fields and no retries for schema violations, and the introduction describes JSON outputs and strict tool use as complementary features usable independently or together.
scopeNote: Structured output is in scope, but the item turns on SDK-specific schema transformations, that minimum and maximum are stripped and additionalProperties is forced to false.

stem: A platform team's agent has grown to several hundred tools spanning many integrations. Definitions now consume a large share of the context window before any work begins, and the agent increasingly picks the wrong tool. The team adds the tool search tool and marks most definitions for deferred loading. Select THREE statements that correctly describe how this arrangement works.

options.text: Every tool definition still travels in the request's tools array; deferred loading marks which of them stay out of the initial context rather than removing them from the request.
Deferred tools are retrieved from an external tool registry at call time, so their schemas no longer need to be supplied with the request and the tools array shrinks to the non-deferred set.
At least one tool must remain non-deferred, normally the tool search tool itself, because something has to be present initially in order to surface the deferred definitions.
Deferring a tool changes where it executes, routing its calls to Anthropic's infrastructure instead of the application that defined it, which no longer runs it.
When a search matches, the API returns references to the matching tools and expands them into full definitions, after which Claude calls the discovered tool in the ordinary way.
The gain is limited to latency, since the definitions still occupy the same amount of context once the request has been assembled, regardless of which tools are used.

explanation: Tool search addresses two problems that arrive together as a tool library grows: definitions crowd the context window, and selection accuracy falls away once several dozen tools are simultaneously available. The mechanism is discovery, not relocation. The application continues to declare every tool it owns, deferred loading keeps the marked ones out of the initial system prompt, and at least one non-deferred tool has to remain so that a search can happen at all. A matching search returns references that the API expands into full definitions on the spot, so only the handful of tools relevant to the current request ever reach the model's context.

distractorNotes.b: There is no external registry in this design. Schemas are still supplied in full with the request, which is what allows the API to expand a match into a complete definition without another round trip.
distractorNotes.d: Deferred loading affects only when a definition enters the model's context. It leaves the execution boundary untouched, so a client tool that is deferred still executes in the application when it is eventually called.
distractorNotes.f: Reducing the context consumed by definitions is the primary purpose. Loading only the few tools a request actually needs cuts the definition footprint substantially and is what keeps selection accuracy from degrading across a large library.

sourceNote: Tool search tool — the 'Context bloat' and 'Tool selection accuracy' points in the introduction, and 'How tool search works'

stem: A team is designing a Model Context Protocol server for an internal knowledge platform. They need three things: read-only document sources that the host application selects and supplies as context, a small set of actions the model may invoke on its own initiative, and named starting templates that a person chooses from a menu. Which mapping onto the server's building blocks is correct?

options.text: The documents are resources, but resources are model-controlled in the same way tools are, so the model pulls them in whenever it judges them relevant and the host makes no selection.
The documents are resources, which the application controls; the actions are tools, which the model controls; the templates are prompts, which the user controls.
All three should be exposed as tools, because tools are the only building block an AI application can discover, and resources and prompts are documentation concepts rather than server features.
The templates should be exposed as tools that return template text, because prompts are chosen by the server rather than offered to a person for selection.

explanation: The three server building blocks differ mainly in who decides when they are used. Tools are model-controlled: the model decides to invoke them based on the request, and they are the way actions get taken. Resources are application-controlled: they are passive, read-only data identified by URI, and the host decides which to retrieve and how to feed them to the model, whether that means passing them wholesale or selecting portions. Prompts are user-controlled: they are reusable templates a person picks to start a piece of work. Matching each requirement to the block with the right control point is the core design decision when building a server.

distractorNotes.a: This misreads the control point for resources. They are passive data sources that the application retrieves and decides how to use, which is what distinguishes them from tools. An application may well enlist AI assistance when choosing which resources to include, but retrieval and control still sit with the application rather than with a model-initiated call.
distractorNotes.c: Resources and prompts are first-class server features with their own discovery and retrieval operations, not documentation. Collapsing everything into tools discards the control distinctions and turns host-curated context and user-selected templates into model-initiated calls.
distractorNotes.d: Prompts exist precisely so that templates can be surfaced for a person to choose, which matches the requirement described. Wrapping them as tools hands the decision to the model instead of the user.

sourceNote: Understanding MCP servers — 'Core Server Features' table, including the 'Who controls it' column, and the 'Tools', 'Resources', and 'Prompts' sections

stem: A backend service is being provisioned to call the Claude API, and the team is deciding how it should authenticate. Which statement about authenticating a request is accurate?

options.text: A request carries either x-api-key or an Authorization header holding a short-lived federated access token, which selects its workspace at token exchange rather than through a workspace header
A request must carry both x-api-key and Authorization together, because the key authenticates the caller while the federated token resolves the particular workspace that the request runs in
An API key is permanent once issued, so rotating a credential means deleting the workspace the key belongs to and recreating both the workspace and the key from scratch
The official client SDKs leave the authentication, version, and content-type headers to the caller, which must set all three by hand on every request it sends to the API

explanation: Authentication takes one of two forms: an API key sent in x-api-key, or a short-lived access token sent in Authorization that the caller obtains through Workload Identity Federation. The two are alternatives, and only one of them is required on a request. The workspace a request runs in is normally selected with a workspace header when a multi-workspace key needs it, but a federated token already carries that choice from the token exchange, so the header is not used with it. Preferring short-lived federated tokens, and otherwise giving each key an expiration and separating environments into their own workspaces, keeps the exposure of any single leaked credential bounded.

distractorNotes.b: The two headers are alternatives, not a pair. An API key is sufficient on its own, and a federated token already identifies both the caller and the workspace the request runs in.
distractorNotes.c: Key type and expiration are both chosen when the key is created, so rotation is a normal key lifecycle operation. Workspaces exist to separate environments and control spend, not as a rotation mechanism.
distractorNotes.d: The SDKs manage those headers automatically, along with retries, streaming, and timeouts. The one header an application may still need to pass itself is the workspace header, and only when its key requires it.

sourceNote: Section "Authentication" header table (one of x-api-key or Authorization is required, the Authorization value being a short-lived access token obtained through Workload Identity Federation; anthropic-workspace-id is required only with a multi-workspace API key and is not used with Workload Identity Federation tokens, which select a workspace at token exchange), section "Getting API keys" (key type and expiration are chosen at creation, and workspaces separate environments and control spend), and section "Client SDKs" (the SDK sends the authentication, version, and content-type headers automatically, while anthropic-workspace-id is passed by the caller when the key needs it).

stem: A team splits a long project CLAUDE.md into smaller markdown files and references them from the main file with the @path import syntax. Which TWO statements correctly describe how those imports behave? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A path written inside backticks or a fenced code block is imported just like one written in prose, so such paths must be removed to avoid unwanted imports.
A relative import path resolves against the file that contains the import, not against the directory Claude Code was launched from.
Imported files are fetched lazily, only when Claude first needs their contents, which keeps the context small at launch.
Imports cannot nest: any @ reference inside an imported file is ignored, so only the imports in the top-level file take effect.
Imported files are expanded and loaded into context at launch, so splitting a file for organization does not by itself reduce context usage.

explanation: Imports use @path/to/import syntax, accept relative or absolute paths, and resolve relative paths against the file containing the import rather than the working directory, so the same import line behaves identically no matter which directory Claude Code was started from. The expansion happens at launch, which is why the guidance to keep each CLAUDE.md short treats imports as an organizational device rather than a way to save context; path-scoped rules are the mechanism for loading instructions only when Claude works with matching files. Imported files may themselves import others, up to a documented maximum depth. One further behaviour is worth knowing: when an import in a project-level memory file resolves outside the working directory, Claude Code shows a one-time approval dialog listing those external files, and declining leaves them disabled.

distractorNotes.a: Import parsing skips markdown code spans and fenced code blocks, so wrapping a path in backticks is the documented way to mention it literally without importing it.
distractorNotes.c: There is no lazy fetch for imports. They are expanded and enter the context window at launch alongside the CLAUDE.md that references them. On-demand loading applies to CLAUDE.md files in subdirectories, which is a different mechanism.
distractorNotes.d: Imported files can recursively import other files, up to a documented maximum depth, so nesting is supported rather than ignored.

sourceNote: Section "Import additional files": "CLAUDE.md files can import additional files using @path/to/import syntax. Imported files are expanded and loaded into context at launch alongside the CLAUDE.md that references them." It continues: "Both relative and absolute paths are allowed. Relative paths resolve relative to the file containing the import, not the working directory. Imported files can recursively import other files" up to a stated maximum depth, and "Import parsing skips Markdown code spans and fenced code blocks. To mention a path in your CLAUDE.md without importing it, wrap it in backticks." The size guidance under "Write effective instructions" notes that content can be split "into imports for organization, though imported files still load and enter the context window at launch", and recommends path-scoped rules when instructions should load only for matching files. The warning in the same section describes the one-time approval dialog for an import in a project-level memory file whose path resolves outside the working directory. Section "How CLAUDE.md files load" separately states that CLAUDE.md files in subdirectories are included when Claude reads files there rather than at launch.

scopeNote: Tests selecting an eval similarity metric (embedding cosine similarity versus exact match, ROUGE-L or a Likert judge). Metric selection appears in no skill objective and is well outside a debugging-and-error-handling item.
stem: An FAQ assistant must give semantically equivalent answers when users ask the same question in different words. The team has assembled fifty groups of paraphrased questions and wants an automated measurement of this criterion. Which approach matches the documented example eval for it?

options.text: Require an exact match between the answers in each group after normalizing whitespace and case, since only identical text proves that the answers are consistent.
Score each answer with ROUGE-L against a reference summary of the source article, averaging the score across the questions in each paraphrase group.
Compute cosine similarity between sentence embeddings of the answers within each paraphrase group, treating values close to 1 as high similarity.
Have an LLM judge rate each answer on a 1 to 5 Likert scale for empathy and professionalism, then compare the ratings within each group.

explanation: The criterion described is consistency: how similar the responses need to be for similar types of input. The documented example eval for consistency uses cosine similarity between sentence embeddings of the model's outputs, where values closer to 1 mean greater similarity, precisely because similar questions should yield semantically similar answers even when the wording varies. The published example is built the same way as the scenario, with paraphrase groups as its test cases. Matching a criterion to a measurement method this way is the point of the example evals: exact match is offered for task fidelity on clear-cut categorical answers, ROUGE-L for relevance and coherence in summarization, an LLM-based Likert scale for tone and style, LLM-based binary classification for privacy preservation, and an LLM-based ordinal scale for context utilization.

distractorNotes.a: Exact match is the documented example for task fidelity on clear-cut, categorical answers. It would fail correct answers that are worded differently, which is exactly what a consistency eval must accept.
distractorNotes.b: ROUGE-L is the documented example for relevance and coherence in summarization, comparing a generated summary with a reference summary; it does not measure agreement between two of the model's own answers.
distractorNotes.d: An LLM-based Likert scale is the documented example for tone and style, rating subjective attributes such as empathy or professionalism, not semantic agreement across paraphrases.

sourceNote: Section "Common success criteria" defines Consistency as "How similar do the model's responses need to be for similar types of input? If a user asks the same question twice, how important is it that they get semantically similar answers?" Section "Example evals" pairs each criterion with a method: "Task fidelity (sentiment analysis) - exact match evaluation" (matching a predefined correct answer "typically after normalizing whitespace and case", "perfect for tasks with clear-cut, categorical answers"); "Consistency (FAQ bot) - cosine similarity evaluation", which "measures the similarity between two vectors (in this case, sentence embeddings of the model's output ...) ... Values closer to 1 indicate higher similarity. It's ideal for evaluating consistency because similar questions should yield semantically similar answers, even if the wording varies", with example test cases of "50 groups with a few paraphrased versions each"; "Relevance and coherence (summarization) - ROUGE-L evaluation", which measures the longest common subsequence "between the candidate and reference summaries"; "Tone and style (customer service) - LLM-based Likert scale", "ideal for evaluating nuanced aspects like empathy, professionalism, or patience"; plus LLM-based binary classification for privacy preservation and an LLM-based ordinal scale for context utilization.

stem: A team asks the model to read a raw support email, decide a category, draft a reply, and translate that reply, all inside one large prompt. Accuracy on the categorisation step is poor and hard to debug. What design change best fits this situation?

options.text: Raise the model's temperature so the single call explores more categorisation options before committing to a final reply.
Split the work into a sequence of calls where each step consumes the previous step's output, with checks between steps.
Merge every instruction into one longer paragraph so nothing about the task can be missed by the model.
Move all of the logic into tool schemas so the model never has to reason about any of the steps itself.

explanation: opt-b is correct because decomposing a task into a chain of smaller calls, where each call handles one easier subtask and its output feeds the next, trades a little latency for higher accuracy and lets you insert programmatic checks (gates) between steps for debugging. opt-a treats a structural problem as a sampling problem; opt-c makes the single overloaded call harder, not easier; opt-d misuses tools, which supply capabilities rather than replacing the model's step-by-step reasoning.

distractorNotes.opt-a: Plausible because temperature affects output variety, but categorisation reliability comes from splitting the task, not from more random sampling.
distractorNotes.opt-c: Plausible because more explicit instructions sometimes help, but concatenating everything keeps the hard, hard-to-inspect single call intact.
distractorNotes.opt-d: Plausible because tools add structure, but tools augment the model rather than remove the need to sequence reasoning steps.

sourceNote: Workflow: Prompt chaining

stem: Deterministic code downstream of the model repeatedly breaks because the JSON it receives is sometimes malformed or missing fields, even after careful prompting. The team is deciding how to harden the boundary between the model's output and their parser. Which statements reflect the intended design? Select TWO.

options.text: The parser should keep adding regexes to repair whatever malformed shapes the model happens to emit each release.
Constraining responses to a supplied schema removes a class of parse-and-retry error handling from the calling code.
Schema constraints are only cosmetic, so the downstream code must still assume arbitrary free-form text on every call.
Constrained output is appropriate exactly where a program, not a human, is the direct consumer of the response.

explanation: opt-b and opt-d are correct: structured outputs constrain the response to a declared schema so calling code gets valid, typed, parseable results and can drop bespoke retry-on-bad-JSON handling, and they are meant for cases where downstream software consumes the output directly. opt-a describes the brittle status quo the feature exists to replace; opt-c is wrong because schema constraints materially change what the model can emit rather than being cosmetic.

distractorNotes.opt-a: Plausible because defensive parsing is common, but the design point is to constrain generation upstream instead of endlessly patching the parser.
distractorNotes.opt-c: Plausible-sounding caution, but incorrect: constrained decoding actually restricts the output shape, so treating it as arbitrary text misses the guarantee.

sourceNote: Why use structured outputs

stem: In a production support system, most incoming questions are simple and repetitive while a small fraction are genuinely complex. The team wants strong quality on the hard cases without paying top-tier cost on every request. Which architecture best fits the constraint?

options.text: Send every request to the smallest model and accept whatever quality it produces on the difficult minority of cases.
Send every request to the largest model so quality is uniformly high across the easy and the hard traffic.
Classify each request first, then dispatch easy traffic to a cheaper model and hard traffic to a more capable one.
Alternate between a cheap and an expensive model on a fixed schedule to average the per-request spend over time.

explanation: opt-c is correct because a routing step that classifies input and directs each class to the appropriately sized model captures most of the cost savings while preserving quality where it matters, a documented multi-model strategy for the cost-to-intelligence tradeoff. opt-a underserves the hard minority; opt-b overpays on the easy majority; opt-d ignores the actual difficulty of each request, so it randomly misroutes hard work to the cheap model.

distractorNotes.opt-a: Plausible as a cost play, but it sacrifices exactly the complex cases the team cares about.
distractorNotes.opt-b: Plausible as a quality play, but it spends top-tier cost on the easy majority the requirement wants to economise.
distractorNotes.opt-d: Plausible because it mixes models, but a schedule uncorrelated with difficulty routes hard cases to the weak model by chance.

sourceNote: Tradeoffs: model choice and multi-model architectures

stem: A team is scoping a new feature and defaults to a fully autonomous agent that plans and directs its own tool use. A reviewer pushes back and asks them to justify the complexity. Which considerations correctly inform whether an autonomous agent is the right choice here? Select TWO.

options.text: Autonomy is the recommended baseline for any Claude feature, and simpler compositions are legacy patterns to avoid.
The simplest thing that works is preferred, with complexity added only when a requirement clearly demands it.
A framework must be adopted first, because agentic behaviour cannot be built by calling the API directly.
Agents trade latency and cost for flexibility, so a predefined workflow is better when the steps are well understood.

explanation: opt-b and opt-d are correct: the guidance is to find the simplest solution and add complexity only when needed, and to reserve autonomous agents for tasks needing model-driven flexibility because agents trade latency and cost for that flexibility, whereas well-defined tasks are better served by predictable workflows. opt-a inverts the guidance, which does not treat autonomy as the default; opt-c is false because many patterns are a few lines against the API directly and a framework is optional.

distractorNotes.opt-a: Plausible given the hype around agents, but the documented stance is to start simple, not to default to autonomy.
distractorNotes.opt-c: Plausible because frameworks exist, but they are optional conveniences, not a prerequisite for agentic behaviour.

sourceNote: When (and when not) to use agents

stem: A coding assistant must change an unpredictable number of files per request, and the set of files and edits cannot be known before the task is examined. The team wants a structure that decides the subtasks at runtime and then combines the results. Which pattern fits best?

options.text: A fixed prompt chain with one predetermined step per file, sized to the largest change the team has seen so far.
A single, larger call that is simply given more context and a higher output cap so it can rewrite every one of the affected files at once.
A parallelisation of a fixed, predefined set of subtasks whose sections are decided up front before the task is read.
An orchestrator that breaks the task down at runtime, delegates each piece to a worker, and synthesises their results.

explanation: opt-d is correct because the orchestrator-workers pattern is designed for tasks where subtasks cannot be predicted in advance: a central call decomposes the work dynamically, delegates to workers, and merges the outputs. opt-a and opt-c both hard-code a fixed set of steps, which the scenario rules out because the number and nature of edits vary per task; opt-b collapses the work into one overloaded call, losing the focused, per-file handling the task needs.

distractorNotes.opt-a: Plausible because chaining is a real pattern, but a fixed chain cannot express a per-request-variable number of subtasks.
distractorNotes.opt-b: Plausible as a shortcut, but one big call forgoes the decomposition that keeps each file's change tractable.
distractorNotes.opt-c: Plausible because it also uses multiple workers, but parallelisation presumes predefined sections, unlike the runtime decomposition required here.

sourceNote: Workflow: Orchestrator-workers

stem: A team is about to start tuning prompts and swapping models to improve a classification feature, but different engineers disagree about whether the current output is even 'good enough'. What should the design put in place before this optimisation work begins?

options.text: Specific, measurable success criteria and an evaluation set, so changes can be judged against a fixed target.
A larger model chosen immediately, because raw capability is what ultimately settles disagreements about quality.
A production rollout to real users first, on the assumption that live feedback replaces the need for defined criteria.
A longer system prompt that describes quality in rich prose, so the model can self-assess whether it did well.

explanation: opt-a is correct because defining specific, measurable success criteria and building evaluations to measure against them is the starting point of the develop-and-refine cycle; without a fixed target, prompt and model changes cannot be judged objectively. opt-b optimises before knowing what 'better' means; opt-c ships without a yardstick and risks user harm while still lacking criteria; opt-d confuses a verbose prompt with an actual measurement method.

distractorNotes.opt-b: Plausible because bigger models can help, but choosing one before defining the target is optimising blind.
distractorNotes.opt-c: Plausible because real feedback is valuable, but it is not a substitute for measurable criteria and can expose users to a poor feature.
distractorNotes.opt-d: Plausible because clear prompts matter, but prose describing quality is not an evaluation and does not measure performance.

sourceNote: Define your success criteria

stem: A team keeps re-typing the same project conventions to Claude Code every session, and also needs one rule that must never be violated regardless of what the model decides. How should responsibility for these two needs be split in the design? Select TWO.

options.text: Durable project conventions belong in a persistent instructions file that is loaded into context at the start of each session.
Both the conventions and the hard rule should be pasted fresh into the chat every session to guarantee they take effect.
A rule that must hold no matter what the model chooses should be enforced by a deterministic hook, not by instruction text.
A hard rule can be guaranteed simply by writing it more firmly in the instructions file, since loaded context is binding.

explanation: opt-a and opt-c are correct: persistent instruction files carry project context into every session so it need not be re-explained, but the model treats loaded instructions as context rather than enforced configuration, so a rule that must always hold should be enforced with a deterministic hook. opt-b ignores the persistence mechanism that exists precisely to avoid re-pasting; opt-d is wrong because stronger wording does not make context binding, which is exactly why a hook is needed.

distractorNotes.opt-b: Plausible as a brute-force habit, but it defeats the purpose of a persistent file and still does not make any rule binding.
distractorNotes.opt-d: Plausible because firm wording feels authoritative, but instructions are guidance, not enforcement, so a hard guarantee needs a hook.

sourceNote: CLAUDE.md vs auto memory

stem: A summariser concatenates the user's fixed instructions with a block of user-submitted article text into one plain-text prompt. Occasionally the model follows directives embedded in the article instead of the real instructions. Which prompt-design change most directly reduces this confusion?

options.text: Shorten the instructions dramatically so the article text clearly dominates the prompt and the model simply focuses on what to summarise.
Repeat the same instructions several times before and after the article so their intent outweighs the embedded text.
Delimit the trusted instructions and the untrusted article in distinct tagged sections so their roles are unambiguous.
Lower the temperature so the model produces a more deterministic summary and is less likely to wander off task.

explanation: opt-c is correct because using structured tags to separate the trusted instructions from the untrusted content makes each part's role explicit and helps the model avoid conflating data with directives. opt-a weakens the very instructions that should govern behaviour; opt-b adds redundancy without drawing a boundary between roles; opt-d changes sampling determinism, which does nothing to clarify which text is an instruction versus data.

distractorNotes.opt-a: Plausible because concise prompts help generally, but cutting the instructions makes them easier, not harder, to override.
distractorNotes.opt-b: Plausible because emphasis can help, but repetition without a structural boundary still mixes instructions and data.
distractorNotes.opt-d: Plausible because temperature affects behaviour, but determinism does not tell the model which span is trusted.

sourceNote: Structure prompts with XML tags

stem: A growing integration exposes many narrow, terse tools (create_pr, review_pr, merge_pr, and dozens more), and the model increasingly picks the wrong one or calls tools at the wrong time. Which design moves are aligned with the guidance on defining tools? Select THREE.

options.text: Give each tool a detailed description covering what it does, when to use it, and when not to, rather than a bare name.
Consolidate closely related operations into fewer, more capable tools instead of one tiny tool per action.
Rely on the tool names alone and trust the model to infer behaviour, keeping descriptions minimal to save tokens.
Use meaningful namespacing in tool names so selection stays unambiguous as the library of tools grows.

explanation: opt-a, opt-b, and opt-d are correct: detailed descriptions are the single biggest factor in tool performance, consolidating related actions into fewer capable tools reduces selection ambiguity, and namespaced names keep selection clear as the surface grows. opt-c is the opposite of the guidance; skimping on descriptions to save tokens removes the very context the model needs to choose and invoke tools correctly.

distractorNotes.opt-c: Plausible because token thrift is a real concern, but starving tools of descriptions directly causes the wrong-tool selection the scenario describes.

sourceNote: Best practices for tool definitions

stem: A translation feature produces serviceable but flat output, and the team notices that when a human reviewer writes specific critiques, a second pass reliably improves the result against clear criteria. They want to bake this into the application. Which pattern and which precondition make it a good fit? Select TWO.

options.text: A parallel voting scheme that runs many identical translations at once and returns whichever variant appears most often.
A loop in which one call produces a draft and another evaluates it and returns feedback for the next revision.
The fit depends on having evaluation criteria clear enough that articulated feedback measurably improves the output.
A single high-effort call, because iterative critique cannot improve a translation beyond the first attempt anyway.

explanation: opt-b and opt-c are correct: the evaluator-optimizer pattern pairs a generator call with an evaluator call that gives feedback in a loop, and it fits precisely when evaluation criteria are clear and articulated feedback demonstrably improves the result, which the scenario reports. opt-a describes voting, which aggregates independent attempts rather than iteratively refining one; opt-d denies the observed improvement from feedback, contradicting the premise.

distractorNotes.opt-a: Plausible because it also uses multiple calls, but voting picks among parallel attempts instead of refining a draft against critique.
distractorNotes.opt-d: Plausible as a simplicity argument, but it contradicts the observed fact that reviewer feedback already improves the second pass.

sourceNote: Workflow: Evaluator-optimizer

stem: A team is adding image understanding to an application that already calls the Messages API. They want to know how images are supplied to a request and how to arrange them relative to the accompanying question. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Images must be trained into a custom model beforehand; the request body itself cannot carry image data of any kind.
Images are provided as image content blocks, and placing the image before the text generally gives better results.
Only a single image is ever allowed per request, and it must always be positioned after all of the text content.
Images can be sent only as public URLs, since embedding image bytes directly in the request is not supported.

explanation: opt-b is correct because vision requests supply images as image content blocks (via base64, a URL, or a Files API file_id), and the guidance is that Claude works best when the image comes before the text. opt-a is false since the request carries the image directly; opt-c invents a single-image, image-last rule that does not exist; opt-d is wrong because base64 and file_id sources are supported alongside URLs.

distractorNotes.opt-a: Plausible to someone thinking of fine-tuning, but vision is a request-time capability and the body carries the image.
distractorNotes.opt-c: Plausible as a guessed constraint, but multiple images are allowed and image-before-text is preferred, not the reverse.
distractorNotes.opt-d: Plausible because URL sources exist, but base64 and file_id sources are equally supported ways to pass an image.

sourceNote: Send images to Claude

stem: For compliance reasons, a company must invoke Claude through its existing Google Cloud vendor account rather than calling Anthropic's API directly. An engineer worries the whole integration must be rebuilt. What is the most accurate characterisation of the change?

options.text: The request format is entirely different, so the messages-based structure of the integration has to be rewritten from scratch.
Going through a cloud vendor is unsupported for production, so requests must still terminate at Anthropic's own endpoint.
Model choice disappears at the vendor, because the platform selects a model automatically for every incoming request.
The interface stays close to the Messages API, with mainly authentication and a few request-format details differing.

explanation: opt-d is correct because accessing Claude through Google Cloud uses an API nearly identical to the Messages API, differing chiefly in how the model is specified, where the version value is passed, and vendor authentication via the official SDK, so the core messages structure carries over. opt-a overstates the change; opt-b is false because vendor access is a supported path; opt-c is wrong because the caller still selects the model, just specified through the endpoint rather than the body.

distractorNotes.opt-a: Plausible if you assume each vendor is bespoke, but the request shape is nearly identical to the Messages API.
distractorNotes.opt-b: Plausible to someone unaware of vendor deployments, but invoking Claude through cloud vendors is fully supported.
distractorNotes.opt-c: Plausible because endpoints encode the model, but the developer still chooses which model to call.

sourceNote: Differences from the Messages API

stem: A data team is integrating the Message Batches API to process a large evaluation set and needs to design how their code submits work and collects answers. Which statements about how the batch workflow behaves are correct? Select TWO.

options.text: Each request in a batch is processed independently, so a batch can mix different kinds of requests together.
The client streams tokens back for every batched request as it runs, exactly as with a synchronous call.
Code submits the batch, then polls for status and retrieves results once processing has ended for the requests.
A batch holds its connection open until finished, blocking the caller until all responses are ready to return.

explanation: opt-a and opt-c are correct: each batched request is handled independently, allowing a mix of request types in one batch, and the workflow is asynchronous, so callers submit, poll for status, and retrieve results after processing ends. opt-b is false because streaming is not supported inside a batch; results come back as a file rather than a live token stream. opt-d contradicts the asynchronous, non-blocking design of batching.

distractorNotes.opt-b: Plausible by analogy to synchronous calls, but stream is unsupported in batch requests and results are returned as a file.
distractorNotes.opt-d: Plausible if you picture a long request, but batching is asynchronous and does not block the caller on an open connection.

sourceNote: How the Message Batches API works

stem: A product manager proposes routing an interactive chat feature's live requests through the Message Batches API to cut cost, since batching is cheaper per token. Users expect a reply within a second or two. Why is this the wrong tool for the workload?

options.text: Batch processing is asynchronous and latency-tolerant, so it does not fit a request that needs an immediate reply.
Batch processing costs more per token than synchronous calls, so it never helps once user wait time is considered.
Batch processing rejects any conversational messages, so a chat turn cannot be expressed as a batched request at all.
Batch processing guarantees sub-second responses but caps throughput too low to serve a busy chat feature's traffic.

explanation: opt-a is correct because the Batches API is an asynchronous, latency-tolerant path suited to work that can wait, which is the opposite of an interactive request needing an immediate response; the realtime-versus-batch tradeoff turns on whether latency matters, not just on price. opt-b misstates pricing, since batching is cheaper per token; opt-c is false because conversational messages can be batched; opt-d inverts the latency profile of batching entirely.

distractorNotes.opt-b: Plausible if you conflate cost with latency, but batching is cheaper per token; the real issue is response time.
distractorNotes.opt-c: Plausible as a guessed limitation, but multi-turn conversational requests can be included in a batch.
distractorNotes.opt-d: Plausible-sounding but backwards: batching is latency-tolerant and asynchronous, not a sub-second path.

sourceNote: When batch processing is useful

stem: An engineer must migrate a large module onto a new internal framework and wants Claude's help without destabilising the codebase. Which approach is safest for a change of this size?

options.text: Have Claude rewrite the whole module in a single pass, then run the full test suite once at the very end.
Let Claude change every call site first and defer running any tests until the new framework is fully wired in.
Split the work into small, behaviour-preserving increments and run the tests after each step before moving on.
Freeze the existing tests during the migration so they cannot fail while the framework is only partly adopted.

explanation: opt-c is correct because a safe large refactor proceeds in small, testable increments that each preserve behaviour, with the suite run between steps so a regression is caught while the change that caused it is still small. The others fail because a single big rewrite (a) makes any failure hard to localise, deferring tests (b) lets defects pile up undetected, and freezing tests (d) removes the very signal that keeps the migration honest.

distractorNotes.a: Plausible because one pass feels efficient, but a whole-module rewrite verified only at the end gives no way to tell which change broke what.
distractorNotes.b: Changing everything before testing sounds orderly, yet it maximises the blast radius and hides regressions until they are expensive to trace.
distractorNotes.d: Silencing tests removes failures cosmetically; it discards the feedback that a behaviour-preserving migration depends on.

sourceNote: Refactor code recipe: tips to refactor in small, testable increments and maintain the same behaviour, verifying with tests

stem: A reviewer is assigned a pull request whose changes were produced with Claude. Which review practices fit the documented guidance for AI-assisted changes? Select TWO.

options.text: Merge without a close read, since a generated diff has already cleared the model's own internal checks.
Read the diff with the same scrutiny applied to any human change before it is allowed to be submitted.
Skip local verification on the basis that the assistant reran the suite while it was producing the change.
Ask Claude to surface the risks and edge cases in its own change so a human can check each of them.

explanation: opt-b and opt-d are correct because AI-generated changes warrant the same review discipline as human ones: read the diff before it is submitted, and use Claude to highlight the risks in its own work so those points get verified rather than trusted. The distractors fail because merging on trust (a) and skipping verification (c) both treat generation as a substitute for review, which the guidance explicitly warns against.

distractorNotes.a: Generated code can still be wrong; treating an internal pass as sufficient skips the human review the guidance calls for before submitting.
distractorNotes.c: Whether the model ran tests while drafting is not a substitute for the reviewer verifying the change in their own environment.

sourceNote: Create pull requests: review Claude's generated PR before submitting and ask Claude to highlight potential risks or considerations

stem: During a task Claude proposes a sweeping set of edits spanning many files, and the developer wants to stay in control of what actually lands. What is the best way to work?

options.text: Let the edits apply straight away, then read the resulting diff and undo whatever looks wrong afterwards.
Review the proposed plan and changes before they touch disk, then apply them in reviewable increments.
Accept every edit at once so the working tree never sits in a half-changed state between the steps.
Disable version-control tracking during the task so the intermediate edits do not clutter the history.

explanation: opt-b is correct because reviewing the plan and diff before changes are written keeps the developer in control and lets edits land in small, reviewable steps. The others fail because applying first and undoing later (a) risks broken intermediate states, accepting everything blindly (c) abandons control for false tidiness, and turning off tracking (d) removes the history that makes incremental review possible.

distractorNotes.a: Undoing after the fact is error-prone and can leave the tree in a broken state; reviewing before edits land avoids that entirely.
distractorNotes.c: Avoiding a half-changed tree is not worth surrendering review; small reviewed increments are precisely the recommended pattern.
distractorNotes.d: Losing version-control history removes the safety net that makes incremental, reviewable changes workable.

sourceNote: Plan before editing: review changes before they touch disk, and refactor in small, testable increments

stem: A developer hits an intermittent failure when running the test command and wants Claude to help find the cause. What gives Claude the best chance of locating the source?

options.text: Tell Claude the bug is somewhere in the codebase and let it search from scratch on its own.
Ask Claude to guess the most likely causes without running anything, purely to save some time.
Describe the symptom in only general terms and request a single fix in one step right away.
Give Claude the exact command that reproduces the failure along with the resulting stack trace.

explanation: opt-d is correct because a concrete reproduction command plus the stack trace gives Claude the specific signal it needs to trace a failure to its source. The others fail because vague framing (a and c) and pure guessing (b) withhold the reproduction detail the documented bug-fixing recipe relies on.

distractorNotes.a: An open-ended search with no reproduction wastes effort; the guidance is to hand over the command and stack trace.
distractorNotes.b: Guessing without reproducing skips the evidence that lets the cause be pinpointed rather than speculated about.
distractorNotes.c: General symptoms give little to work from; a precise reproduction and trace are what narrow the search.

sourceNote: Fix bugs efficiently: tell Claude the command to reproduce the issue and get a stack trace

stem: A developer asks Claude to add tests to a service that currently has none. Which expectations match how Claude approaches writing those tests? Select TWO.

options.text: It reads the existing test files and follows the style, frameworks and assertions already in use.
It swaps out the project's test framework for whichever one it currently judges to be strongest.
It can surface edge cases and error conditions that are easy for a person to overlook when asked.
It guarantees complete branch coverage with no need to run the resulting tests to confirm them.

explanation: opt-a and opt-c are correct because Claude examines existing test files to match their conventions and, when prompted, can suggest edge cases and error conditions a person might miss. The distractors fail because it works within your existing framework rather than replacing it (b), and generated tests still have to be run to be trusted (d).

distractorNotes.b: The guidance is to match existing frameworks and patterns, not to replace a team's chosen test framework on its own initiative.
distractorNotes.d: No coverage guarantee is implied, and the recipe explicitly ends by running the new tests and fixing failures.

sourceNote: Work with tests: Claude examines existing test files to match style and frameworks, can suggest edge cases, and you run and verify the tests

stem: A team wants to run Claude as a non-interactive step inside their continuous-integration pipeline to process changes in batch. Which characterisation of this use is accurate?

options.text: Claude can be piped into scripts so it runs headless, which suits CI and batch processing.
Claude only works inside an interactive terminal and cannot be scripted into a pipeline at all.
Running Claude under CI first requires switching off every one of its file-editing abilities.
Batch use forces each individual request through a separate manual approval before it can run.

explanation: opt-a is correct because Claude can be piped into scripts to run headless, which is exactly the pattern documented for CI and batch processing. The others fail because it is not confined to an interactive terminal (b), CI use does not require disabling editing (c), and headless batch runs are not gated on per-request manual approval (d).

distractorNotes.b: This contradicts the documented headless mode, where Claude is piped into scripts precisely so it runs without a terminal.
distractorNotes.c: Nothing about CI requires stripping editing abilities; headless mode is about scripting, not disabling tools.
distractorNotes.d: Manual per-request approval would defeat batch use; the documented pattern is unattended scripted execution.

sourceNote: Pipe Claude into scripts for CI and batch processing

stem: Two developers want to run separate Claude sessions against the same repository at the same time without their edits colliding. What is the recommended setup?

options.text: Point both sessions at one shared working copy and coordinate by taking turns editing the files.
Run only one session at a time, since concurrent sessions on a repository always corrupt its state.
Use separate git worktrees so each session operates in its own checkout and edits cannot collide.
Disable file writes in one of the two sessions so that only a single session ever changes code.

explanation: opt-c is correct because git worktrees give each session an isolated checkout, letting parallel work proceed without colliding edits. The others fail because sharing one working copy (a) invites collisions, serialising to one session (b) needlessly forgoes parallelism, and muting one session's writes (d) defeats the goal of two developers working at once.

distractorNotes.a: A single shared checkout is exactly what causes the collisions; taking turns just serialises the work by hand.
distractorNotes.b: Concurrent sessions do not inevitably corrupt a repo; worktrees are the documented way to run them safely in parallel.
distractorNotes.d: Blocking one session's writes removes the parallelism the developers wanted rather than enabling it.

sourceNote: Run parallel sessions with worktrees so concurrent edits don't collide

stem: A team commits shared settings in the project settings file, but one developer needs a different model for that project only, without changing it for teammates. Which statement about how the configuration layers resolve is correct?

options.text: User settings in the home directory outrank the shared project file, so the home value wins here.
The shared project file always wins, so a per-developer override for a single project is impossible.
Only an organisation-managed file is able to change a value that the shared project file has set.
A project-local file overrides the shared file, so that developer sets the value there for their own sessions.

explanation: opt-d is correct because project-local settings sit above the shared project file in precedence, so a personal per-project override lives there and affects only that developer. The others fail because user settings rank below the shared project file (a), per-developer overrides are supported rather than impossible (b), and it takes a local file, not only a managed one, to override the shared value (c).

distractorNotes.a: Precedence runs the other way for these two: the shared project file outranks user settings, so a home-directory value does not win.
distractorNotes.b: A local override for one project is exactly the supported mechanism, so the shared file does not always win.
distractorNotes.c: Managed settings are not the only higher layer; a developer's own project-local file already overrides the shared value.

sourceNote: Settings precedence and Keep personal settings out of a repository: project-local overrides shared project, which overrides user

stem: A developer is deciding where a new instruction belongs. It is a build-and-test convention every teammate on the project should follow. Which placement fits the intended scope, and why?

options.text: The personal user memory file, because instructions are said to load more reliably from the home directory.
The project memory file, because it is a shared team standard distributed to everyone through version control.
A git-ignored local file, so each teammate maintains a personal copy and keeps them aligned by hand.
The personal user memory file, so the convention automatically applies across every project the developer opens.

explanation: opt-b is correct because a convention the whole team must follow belongs in the project memory file, which is shared through source control so everyone gets it. The others fail because the user file is personal and per-developer (a and d) and a git-ignored local file is not shared at all, forcing brittle manual syncing (c).

distractorNotes.a: Load reliability does not depend on the home directory; the deciding factor is scope, and a team standard is project-scoped.
distractorNotes.c: A local, ignored file is explicitly personal; using it for a team standard means it never reaches teammates automatically.
distractorNotes.d: The user file would leak this project's convention into unrelated projects, which is broader than the intended scope.

sourceNote: Choose where to put CLAUDE.md files: project instructions are shared with the team via source control; user instructions are personal across projects

stem: A developer wants to keep some Claude configuration private to their own machine while still committing the team's shared setup. Which items should be kept out of version control? Select TWO.

options.text: The project memory file holding the team's architecture notes and shared coding standards.
The local settings file carrying personal, single-project overrides and standing approvals.
The shared project settings file that defines the team's agreed permissions and hooks.
Personal scratch values such as sandbox URLs and preferred test data used in one project.

explanation: opt-b and opt-d are correct because the local settings file and personal scratch values (sandbox URLs, test data) are individual, per-project preferences that are meant to stay out of git. The distractors fail because the project memory file (a) and the shared project settings file (c) are exactly what a team commits so everyone shares the same setup.

distractorNotes.a: Team architecture notes and standards are meant to be shared through source control, so this belongs in the repository.
distractorNotes.c: Shared permissions and hooks are committed precisely so every teammate who clones the repo gets the same setup.

sourceNote: Keep personal settings out of a repository and Share settings with your team: local file stays out of git; shared settings.json is committed

stem: A team finds that regenerating a year-old report yields different results over time from identical inputs, and traces it to the model their configuration resolves to. Which practice most directly addresses this?

options.text: Pin an explicit model version in config so runs stay reproducible until a deliberate upgrade.
Raise the output ceiling so the model has more room to return a complete answer on each run.
Switch to whichever model is newest on every run so results always reflect the latest quality.
Remove the model from configuration and let each environment resolve its own default instead.

explanation: opt-a is correct because pinning an explicit model version keeps behaviour stable across runs, so results are reproducible until the team chooses to migrate. The others fail because the output ceiling does not govern which model answers (b), always taking the newest model guarantees drift rather than stability (c), and deferring to per-environment defaults makes results depend on where the job runs (d).

distractorNotes.b: The output ceiling changes how much text can return, not which model runs, so it does not stop version-driven drift.
distractorNotes.c: Chasing the newest model on every run is the opposite of reproducibility; it introduces exactly the variation being seen.
distractorNotes.d: Letting each environment pick a default makes outputs depend on the environment, worsening rather than fixing the drift.

sourceNote: Overview and Migrating to replacements: models change over their lifecycle, so migrations are deliberate and tested rather than automatic

stem: A developer has skills and hooks in their local Claude directory that several teams now want to reuse and version. Which statements about packaging this as a plugin are accurate? Select TWO.

options.text: Setting a version on the plugin means users receive updates only when that version field is bumped.
Standalone local configuration is the recommended channel for distributing config across many teams.
A plugin cannot declare its own version, so every consumer always tracks the latest commit by default.
Packaging it as a versioned plugin suits sharing and reuse better than copying the local files around.

explanation: opt-a and opt-d are correct because a plugin's version field gates when consumers receive updates, and a versioned plugin is the recommended way to share and reuse configuration across teams. The distractors fail because standalone local config is meant for personal or single-project use rather than wide distribution (b), and a plugin can indeed set an explicit version (c).

distractorNotes.b: Standalone local configuration suits personal and project-specific use; sharing across teams is what plugins and marketplaces are for.
distractorNotes.c: This is backwards: a plugin can declare a version, and doing so is what controls when consumers get updates.

sourceNote: When to use plugins vs standalone configuration, and the version field: users only receive updates when the version is bumped

stem: A developer keeps adding rules to the project memory file expecting them to be enforced like hard constraints, and is surprised when Claude occasionally deviates. Which statements reflect how these files are designed to work? Select TWO.

options.text: Memory-file entries are enforced constraints, so any deviation from one is always a parsing bug.
The memory file is loaded as context that guides behaviour rather than strictly enforcing it.
To hard-block an action regardless of what the model decides, a hook is the right mechanism.
Files load most-specific first, so a narrow rule always overrides a broader one by strict rule.

explanation: opt-b and opt-c are correct because memory files are treated as context that guides Claude rather than enforced configuration, and blocking an action regardless of the model's choice is a job for a hook. The distractors fail because deviation is not a parsing bug but a consequence of context not being a hard constraint (a), and load order runs broadest-first with no guarantee that a narrower entry strictly overrides a broader one (d).

distractorNotes.a: Because entries are guidance rather than enforced rules, occasional deviation is expected behaviour, not evidence of a parse error.
distractorNotes.d: Files load from broadest to most specific, and since they are context rather than strict precedence, a narrow rule is not guaranteed to override a broad one.

sourceNote: CLAUDE.md vs auto memory: files are treated as context, not enforced configuration; use a PreToolUse hook to block an action

stem: A business goal states that a support assistant must answer accurately and stay responsive under load. A developer is separating this into requirement types before design begins. Which reading is correct?

options.text: Both clauses are functional requirements, because each one describes something a user can directly observe.
Both clauses are non-functional, because the answers an assistant produces are never a functional concern.
Answer accuracy is a functional requirement, while responsiveness under load is a non-functional one.
Neither counts as a requirement until a number is attached, so both stay out of scope for the moment.

explanation: opt-c is correct because accuracy describes what the system must do (functional), while responsiveness under load is an operational quality of how it performs (non-functional). The others fail because they collapse the two categories together (a and b) or deny that an as-yet-unquantified goal is a requirement at all (d), when the task is precisely to classify then make it measurable.

distractorNotes.a: Observability does not make both functional; responsiveness under load is an operational quality attribute, which is non-functional.
distractorNotes.b: Answer accuracy is a core functional requirement describing what the assistant must do, so treating both as non-functional is wrong.
distractorNotes.d: A goal is still a requirement before it is quantified; the next step is to make it measurable, not to set it aside.

sourceNote: Define your success criteria: task-fidelity criteria versus operational metrics such as response time and uptime

stem: A stakeholder gives only the business aim to pick a model that keeps costs sane while handling the hardest tickets. Which criteria should the team derive to turn this into something decidable? Select TWO.

options.text: The capability level that the hardest tickets actually demand from any candidate model.
The exact per-token price of every model the vendor has ever published, held from memory.
A budget for development and production usage that the chosen model has to fit within.
The colour theme and editor mode each developer happens to prefer during the evaluation.

explanation: opt-a and opt-c are correct because the documented starting criteria for choosing a model are the capabilities the task demands and the cost budget for development and production; both turn a vague aim into decidable requirements. The distractors fail because memorising every historical price (b) is trivia rather than a criterion, and personal UI preferences (d) are irrelevant to model selection.

distractorNotes.b: A precise recall of all historical prices is not a decision criterion; the relevant factor is a cost budget the model must fit.
distractorNotes.d: Theme and editor preferences have nothing to do with matching a model to business needs; they are unrelated to the requirement.

sourceNote: Establish key criteria: capabilities, speed, and cost when choosing a model

stem: A service has run in production for a year on a model that was just marked deprecated with a retirement date. Which operate-and-maintain action best fits managing the system across the model lifecycle?

options.text: Wait until requests start failing, then swap models reactively once the outage becomes visible.
Test a recommended replacement well before the retirement date and migrate ahead of that date.
Assume deprecated status is merely cosmetic and keep the current model indefinitely without change.
Pin the deprecated model harder so the platform is unable to move the workload off it later on.

explanation: opt-b is correct because the documented maintenance practice is to test a recommended replacement ahead of the retirement date and migrate before requests to the retired model start failing. The others fail because waiting for failures invites an avoidable outage (a), treating deprecation as cosmetic ignores the scheduled retirement (c), and there is no way to pin past a retirement date, since retired-model requests simply fail (d).

distractorNotes.a: Reacting only after failures means an outage that the notice period and pre-retirement testing were meant to prevent.
distractorNotes.c: Deprecation is not cosmetic; a retirement date is set, after which requests to the model fail, so inaction is unsafe.
distractorNotes.d: No configuration keeps a retired model alive; once retired, requests fail regardless of how firmly it was pinned.

sourceNote: Migrating to replacements and Best practices: test replacements before the retirement date; requests to retired models fail

stem: A team caches Claude's answers keyed on the exact prompt string and sets temperature to 0, expecting identical inputs to always return byte-identical outputs so the cache can never serve a mismatched result. In testing they occasionally see two different completions for the same input. What best explains this?

options.text: Temperature 0 fully disables sampling, so any variation must come from an unnoticed change in the prompt text actually being sent.
Even at temperature 0 the API is not fully deterministic, so identical inputs can differ and exact-match caching cannot assume reproducible replies.
Temperature 0 only fixes the first token and leaves later tokens free to vary, so capping max_tokens at 1 would restore full determinism.
Determinism holds only when top_p is also pinned to 0, so adding that single sampling parameter will make repeated calls come out identical.

explanation: opt-b is correct: Anthropic documents that even with temperature set to 0 the results are not fully deterministic and identical inputs may produce different outputs across calls, so a cache keyed on exact input cannot assume the response is reproducible byte-for-byte. opt-a wrongly treats temperature 0 as a determinism guarantee and blames the prompt. opt-c invents a first-token-only rule. opt-d invents a top_p condition; neither parameter makes the service fully deterministic.

distractorNotes.opt-a: Plausible because temperature 0 does bias toward the most probable tokens, but it is not a determinism guarantee, so unexplained variation is expected, not necessarily a changed prompt.
distractorNotes.opt-c: Plausible-sounding mechanics, but temperature does not act on only the first token, and shrinking max_tokens does not remove non-determinism.
distractorNotes.opt-d: top_p is a sampling control, not a determinism switch; setting it to 0 does not make repeated calls identical.

sourceNote: Temperature (note on non-determinism at temperature 0)

stem: A service sends very long documents to Claude and also sets a high max_tokens because it wants a long answer. On the longest inputs the model runs out of room to finish its response. A developer argues that input and output draw from separate budgets, so the input size should not matter. How does the context window actually work?

options.text: Input tokens and generated output tokens count against independent limits, so a large input never constrains how much the model can produce in reply.
Only the system prompt and tool definitions count toward the window, while ordinary user messages and the response are tracked in a separate pool.
The context window is one working-memory budget shared by the whole request and the response, so a large input leaves less room for output.
The window measures the prompt alone, and because the reply is streamed out afterward it does not occupy the same budget as the input.

explanation: opt-c is correct: the context window is the model's working memory covering all the text it can reference including the response itself, so the system prompt, every message, tool definitions, and the generated output all share one budget; a large input therefore leaves less room to generate. opt-a, opt-b, and opt-d all imagine separate budgets, but input and output are counted against the same window.

distractorNotes.opt-a: Plausible because input and output are reported as distinct usage fields, but they are billed distinctly, not budgeted separately; both draw on the same window.
distractorNotes.opt-b: Everything in the request counts toward the window, including ordinary user messages and the generated response, not just system prompt and tools.
distractorNotes.opt-d: Streaming only changes how the response is delivered; the generated tokens still occupy the same context window.

sourceNote: How the context window works (window holds history plus the new output)

stem: A team is deciding which features should run with thinking enabled. They want to spend the extra thinking tokens only where they actually change the outcome. Which TWO statements reflect sound use of thinking? Select TWO.

options.text: Thinking should be enabled everywhere, because spending more thinking tokens reliably raises answer quality on every kind of task.
Heavier thinking is best reserved for tasks that need multi-step reasoning, where the extra tokens buy a meaningfully better answer.
Thinking tokens are free in practice, since they are not billed as output and do not count toward the context window.
For simple, low-ambiguity tasks, keeping thinking low avoids paying latency and token cost for reasoning the task does not need.

explanation: opt-b and opt-d are correct: thinking earns its cost on genuinely hard, multi-step problems, while on simple tasks it mainly adds latency and spend, so match thinking depth to difficulty. opt-a is wrong because more thinking is not universally better and wastes budget on easy tasks. opt-c is wrong because thinking tokens are billed as output tokens and do count toward the context window, so they are a real cost to weigh.

distractorNotes.opt-a: Plausible because thinking helps on hard problems, but enabling it globally pays cost on tasks that gain nothing from it.
distractorNotes.opt-c: Thinking tokens are billed as output and count toward the context window, so treating them as free misjudges the tradeoff.

sourceNote: The context window with thinking (thinking tokens billed as output, count toward the window)

stem: An extraction feature returns correct facts but in inconsistent formats, and a downstream parser keeps choking on the variation. The prompt already describes the desired schema in prose. A developer proposes adding a few worked input/output examples. What does multi-shot prompting primarily buy in this situation?

options.text: Concrete examples steer the output's format and structure toward a consistent shape, matching the inconsistency the parser hits.
Examples expand the model's underlying factual knowledge, so the extracted facts themselves come back more accurate than before.
Examples cut token usage, because once shown a pattern the model can skip reading the prose instructions on later calls.
Examples make the model deterministic, guaranteeing byte-identical output for every single input that happens to share the same shape.

explanation: opt-a is correct: worked examples (few-shot or multi-shot prompting) are one of the most reliable ways to steer output format, tone, and structure, directly addressing inconsistent shape. opt-b overstates examples as knowledge injection rather than format steering. opt-c invents a token saving; the instructions are still sent each call. opt-d wrongly promises determinism, which examples do not provide.

distractorNotes.opt-b: Examples shape output form and style; they do not add new factual knowledge to the model.
distractorNotes.opt-c: Each request is independent, so the prose still costs tokens; examples add input rather than removing it.
distractorNotes.opt-d: Examples improve consistency but do not make generation deterministic across calls.

sourceNote: Use examples effectively (few-shot/multishot steers format, tone, structure)

stem: A team debates whether every prompt should carry examples. They want a principled rule for when examples earn their place versus a plain zero-shot prompt. Which TWO statements are sound? Select TWO.

options.text: When output must follow a specific format, tone, or structure, a handful of well-chosen examples is among the most reliable ways to get consistency.
Examples are always required, because a zero-shot prompt cannot produce usable output for any non-trivial task at all.
For a simple, unambiguous instruction the model already handles well, a clear zero-shot prompt can suffice and avoids the extra input tokens.
More examples strictly improve results, so packing in dozens is always better than including only a few of them.

explanation: opt-a and opt-c are correct: examples shine when format or structure matters, but a clear zero-shot prompt can be enough for simple, well-handled tasks, and it avoids extra tokens. opt-b is false because zero-shot prompts routinely work for straightforward tasks. opt-d is false because the guidance recommends a small set (about three to five) rather than piling on dozens.

distractorNotes.opt-b: Zero-shot prompts work well for many clear tasks, so examples are not universally required.
distractorNotes.opt-d: Guidance is to include a few strong examples, not dozens; more is not monotonically better.

sourceNote: Use examples effectively (include 3-5 examples; examples steer consistency)

stem: A developer new to Claude assumes one token equals one character and sizes their limits by counting characters, then is surprised the numbers do not line up with reported usage. Which understanding of tokens is correct?

options.text: A token is always exactly one whole word, so the token count simply equals the number of space-separated words present in the text.
A token is always a fixed number of bytes, so dividing the byte length by that constant yields the exact token count.
Tokens map one-to-one onto characters, so character count and token count are interchangeable for sizing purposes.
Tokens are sub-word units that may be words, subwords, or characters, so token count only approximately tracks character count.
