explanation: opt-d is correct: tokens are the model's smallest units and may correspond to words, subwords, characters, or bytes, so a token roughly maps to a few characters and the ratio shifts with the language and content. opt-a, opt-b, and opt-c each assume a fixed one-to-one mapping (to words, bytes, or characters), which is why the developer's character-based sizing does not match.

distractorNotes.opt-a: Tokens are not whole words; common words may be one token while others split into several.
distractorNotes.opt-b: There is no fixed bytes-per-token constant; tokenization depends on the text.
distractorNotes.opt-c: Tokens do not map one-to-one to characters, which is exactly why the counts diverged.

sourceNote: Tokens (smallest units: words, subwords, characters, or bytes)

stem: A team is starting a Python integration and debates whether to hand-roll HTTP calls to the Messages endpoint or adopt Anthropic's official client SDK. What is the most accurate framing of what the official client SDK provides?

options.text: The SDK runs the full agent loop and executes tools for you, so you no longer send individual requests or handle their responses at all.
The SDK swaps the REST API for a different wire protocol, so requests no longer correspond to the documented HTTP endpoints and shapes.
The SDK is an idiomatic client over the same REST API, adding type safety plus built-in streaming, retries, and error handling.
The SDK is only a thin set of type stubs, so features like streaming and retries must still be implemented by hand on top of it.

explanation: opt-c is correct: the client SDKs are general-purpose Messages API clients that wrap the same REST API with idiomatic interfaces, type safety, and built-in streaming, retries, and error handling, while you still send each request. opt-a describes the higher-level Agent SDK, not the client SDK. opt-b is wrong because the SDK still targets the documented REST endpoints. opt-d understates the SDK, which provides those features rather than leaving them to you.

distractorNotes.opt-a: Running the agent loop and executing tools describes the Claude Agent SDK, not the request/response client SDK.
distractorNotes.opt-b: The SDK is a client over the existing REST API; it does not replace the HTTP protocol.
distractorNotes.opt-d: Streaming, retries, and error handling are built in, so they are not left for the team to implement.

sourceNote: Client SDKs (idiomatic interfaces, type safety, built-in streaming, retries, error handling)

stem: An interactive chat app enables streaming, and someone predicts it will lower the monthly bill by reducing how many tokens each response consumes. Is that the right expectation about what streaming does?

options.text: Yes; streaming sends tokens incrementally, and those partial tokens are billed at a lower per-token rate than one batched response.
No; streaming delivers the same response incrementally over server-sent events, improving perceived responsiveness but not token cost.
Yes; streaming lets the client stop early on most requests, so the average response ends up billed for far fewer output tokens overall.
No; streaming actually costs more, because each server-sent event in the stream is billed as though it were a wholly separate request.

explanation: opt-b is correct: streaming uses server-sent events to deliver the same response incrementally, which improves perceived latency and time-to-first-token but does not change how many tokens are generated or what they cost. opt-a and opt-c invent billing discounts from streaming or early stopping. opt-d invents a per-event surcharge. Streaming is a delivery mechanism, not a pricing lever.

distractorNotes.opt-a: There is no lower per-token rate for streamed tokens; delivery method does not change token pricing.
distractorNotes.opt-c: Early client-side stopping is not the point of streaming, and it is not how streaming reduces the bill.
distractorNotes.opt-d: Server-sent events are parts of one response, not separate billable requests.

sourceNote: Streaming messages (incremental delivery via server-sent events)

stem: A team adds streaming so the UI can show Claude's answer as it is produced. Which TWO statements about how streaming works with the SDKs are accurate? Select TWO.

options.text: Streaming returns the whole response in a single final event, so the interface still waits for generation to finish before it can show anything.
The response arrives as a sequence of incremental server-sent events, which the client can render as they come in.
For very large max_tokens generations the SDKs recommend streaming to avoid hitting HTTP request timeouts.
Streaming requires opening and managing a persistent websocket, kept separate from the ordinary request path.

explanation: opt-b and opt-c are correct: streaming delivers the response as incremental server-sent events the client renders progressively, and the SDKs recommend streaming for very large max_tokens generations so long responses do not exceed HTTP timeouts. opt-a contradicts incremental delivery. opt-d is wrong because streaming uses server-sent events over the normal request, not a separately managed websocket.

distractorNotes.opt-a: Streaming exists precisely so the UI does not wait for the full response; events arrive during generation.
distractorNotes.opt-d: Streaming uses server-sent events on the standard request, not a persistent websocket the team must manage.

sourceNote: Streaming messages (SSE deltas; streaming recommended for large max_tokens to avoid timeouts)

stem: A developer builds multi-turn chat and assumes that after the first request the service remembers the conversation, so later requests can send only the newest user message. Earlier context then starts disappearing from responses. What is the correct model of how the Messages API handles conversation state?

options.text: The API keeps a server-side session per API key, so omitting earlier turns should not lose context and the real bug must be elsewhere.
The API stores the last several turns automatically and only forgets once a session times out, so lengthening that timeout fixes the loss.
The API reconstructs missing history from the API key's recent activity, so prior turns need not be resent on each request.
Each request is self-contained, so the app must resend the prior conversation every turn since the API does not retain it between calls.

explanation: opt-d is correct: each request's input must contain all previous conversation history plus the current user message, because the Messages API does not persist state between calls; the client owns the transcript and resends it each turn. opt-a, opt-b, and opt-c all assume some server-side memory keyed to a session or API key, which does not exist, so dropping earlier turns is exactly why context is lost.

distractorNotes.opt-a: There is no per-key server session; omitting earlier turns really does drop that context.
distractorNotes.opt-b: The API does not automatically retain recent turns, so no timeout setting brings them back.
distractorNotes.opt-c: History is not reconstructed from account activity; it must be resent explicitly in messages.

sourceNote: Input-output flow (input phase contains all previous conversation history plus the current user message)

stem: A team hand-rolled HTTP calls and now sees intermittent rate-limit and server errors under load, which they handle by immediately retrying in a tight loop. They are considering the official SDK. Which TWO points correctly describe robust request handling and what the SDK offers? Select TWO.

options.text: Transient failures should be retried as fast as possible with no delay, since any backoff only slows the recovery down.
A single failed request means the workload must halt, because retrying any request risks duplicate side effects in every case.
A 429 carries a retry-after hint, so transient errors are best retried after waiting rather than in a tight loop.
The official SDKs include automatic retries, moving that logic into the library instead of code the team maintains by hand.

explanation: opt-c and opt-d are correct: rate-limit responses return a retry-after header indicating how long to wait, so transient errors should be retried after backing off, and the official SDKs perform automatic retries so the team need not hand-roll that logic. opt-a is wrong because a tight no-delay retry loop worsens rate limiting. opt-b overgeneralizes; transient errors are routinely retried rather than forcing the workload to stop.

distractorNotes.opt-a: Immediate no-delay retries hammer the API and prolong rate limiting; backoff is the correct response.
distractorNotes.opt-b: Transient rate-limit and server errors are safely retried; halting the whole workload is not required.

sourceNote: 429 handling (retry-after header; SDKs' automatic retries)

stem: A retrieval pipeline batches a variable number of source documents into each prompt, and occasionally a batch is large enough to be rejected. The team would rather catch an oversize batch while assembling it than learn about it from a failed call. Which approach fits?

options.text: Estimate the request's token size with the token counting API before sending, and trim or split when the estimate nears the window.
Send the request as-is and rely on the model to silently truncate the oldest content so that the call always fits within the window.
Assume a fixed characters-per-token ratio is exact and hard-code a character cap, since token counts never vary with the actual content.
Set max_tokens as high as possible, which reserves extra window space and thereby prevents any oversize input from failing.

explanation: opt-a is correct: the token counting API lets you estimate a request before sending it, so the service can measure assembled prompts and trim or split when they approach the window. opt-b is wrong because the API does not silently truncate to fit. opt-c is wrong because token counts vary by content, so a hard-coded character cap is unreliable. opt-d misreads max_tokens, which reserves output room and does not shield an oversize input.

distractorNotes.opt-b: The request is not silently truncated to fit; an oversize request is an error to prevent, not a quiet trim.
distractorNotes.opt-c: Characters-per-token is only approximate and shifts with content and language, so a fixed cap misjudges size.
distractorNotes.opt-d: max_tokens governs output length and consumes window space; raising it does not accommodate a larger input.

sourceNote: How the context window works (estimate a request before sending with the token counting API)

stem: A team is choosing between Anthropic's client SDKs and the Claude Agent SDK for a new build. Which TWO statements correctly distinguish the two levels of tooling? Select TWO.

options.text: The client SDKs are Messages API clients where you send each request and handle each response yourself.
The client SDKs and the Agent SDK are the same tool under two names, so the choice between them is purely cosmetic.
The Agent SDK is only a set of type definitions layered on the client SDK, so it adds no runtime behavior of its own.
The Agent SDK operates at a higher level, providing the agent loop, tool execution, and runtime rather than raw request/response.

explanation: opt-a and opt-d are correct: the client SDKs are for calling the API yourself, issuing each request and handling each response, whereas the Agent SDK works at a higher level and provides the agent loop, tool execution, and runtime. opt-b is wrong because they are distinct tools at different levels. opt-c is wrong because the Agent SDK supplies real runtime behavior, not just types.

distractorNotes.opt-b: They are different tools at different levels of abstraction, so the choice is substantive, not cosmetic.
distractorNotes.opt-c: The Agent SDK provides the agent loop and runtime, which is behavior, not merely type definitions.

sourceNote: Building agents or using Claude Code? (client SDK vs Agent SDK levels)

stem: A team upgrades to a newer Claude model expecting a drop-in improvement and reuses prompts tuned for the previous generation. Some outputs regress in format and length. What does Anthropic's guidance advise about selecting or moving between models?

options.text: Newer models are strict supersets of older ones, so any regression has to be an infrastructure bug rather than a model difference.
Treat a model change as something to validate: run benchmark tests with real prompts and data, since behavior shifts across releases.
Prompt wording never interacts with the model version, so re-testing prompts after an upgrade is wasted effort that can be skipped.
Always pick the largest available model to eliminate behavior differences, since capability gaps are the only real source of any regressions.

explanation: opt-b is correct: Anthropic advises deciding whether to upgrade or change models by creating benchmark tests specific to your use case and testing with your actual prompts and data, because behavior can change across releases and prompts tuned for one model may need adjustment on another. opt-a and opt-c wrongly assume model versions are interchangeable for a given prompt. opt-d wrongly treats model size as a way to avoid behavior differences instead of evaluating them.

distractorNotes.opt-a: Newer models are not guaranteed supersets; behavior genuinely shifts across releases, so regressions can be real model differences.
distractorNotes.opt-c: Prompts often interact with model version, so re-evaluating after an upgrade is exactly what is recommended.
distractorNotes.opt-d: Choosing the largest model does not neutralize cross-release behavior changes and ignores cost and latency tradeoffs.

sourceNote: Decide whether to upgrade or change models (benchmark with your actual prompts and data)

stem: During a large refactoring task, the main agent has to survey dozens of files before making any change, and its context fills with file contents long before the edits begin. The team wants the survey done without crowding out the working conversation. What is the best way to structure this?

options.text: Delegate the survey to a subagent, whose file reads stay in its own context so only a summary returns.
Raise the main agent's max-turns option so it has room to read every file in one conversation.
Enlarge the context window through a query option so all of the surveyed files fit in the conversation.
Lower the agent's reasoning effort so each turn spends fewer tokens and more file content fits.

explanation: opt-a is correct: a subagent runs in isolated context, so its intermediate reads and tool results stay inside it and only the final summary returns to the parent, keeping the main conversation clean. The others don't stop the accumulation: more turns still store the same content, the context window is not a size you raise, and effort changes reasoning not retained history.

distractorNotes.opt-b: Plausible because more turns lets it read more, but max-turns governs tool-use round trips, not how much history the context holds; the file content still accumulates.
distractorNotes.opt-c: Plausible-sounding, but the context window is a fixed property of the model, not a lever you enlarge through options.
distractorNotes.opt-d: Effort controls how much the model reasons per turn, not how much prior tool output remains in context.

sourceNote: Benefits of using subagents — Context isolation

stem: A team adds a subagent that audits code for problems and reports them. Reviewers worry it might accidentally change the files it inspects. What is the most reliable way to guarantee it cannot?

options.text: Instruct the subagent in its system prompt to review only and never edit, and rely on it to comply.
Define the subagent with only read and search tools, so editing a file is not an action available to it.
Give the subagent a more capable model, which is less likely to make an unintended change while reviewing.
Let it run normally, then inspect the resulting diff and revert any edits it should not have made.

explanation: opt-b is correct: restricting the subagent to read and search tools removes any write capability, so modification is impossible by construction rather than by request. Prompt instructions are guidance a model can be steered around, model capability doesn't remove the write tool, and reverting afterwards is detective rather than preventive.

distractorNotes.opt-a: Plausible because a clear instruction usually works, but a system prompt is not an enforceable boundary; the tool stays available if the model chooses it.
distractorNotes.opt-c: A more capable model can still call a write tool; capability does not remove the ability to edit.
distractorNotes.opt-d: Reverting after the fact still means the change happened and any side effects already occurred.

sourceNote: Benefits of using subagents — Tool restrictions

stem: A team is deciding how tightly to scope the tool set they grant an autonomous agent that will process untrusted content. Select TWO statements that correctly describe what restricting the agent to a minimal tool set achieves.

options.text: The shorter tool list mainly makes the agent respond faster, which is the primary security reason to trim it.
If injected instructions try to steer the agent, it can still only take actions its granted tools expose, limiting harm.
A minimal tool set removes the need to keep untrusted input separated from the agent's trusted instructions.
Narrowing tools to the task means an unintended or injected instruction has fewer actions available to reach for.
With tools restricted, no human-approval step is ever needed, because nothing the agent can do is harmful.

explanation: opt-b and opt-d are correct: least privilege limits the actions available to the agent, so even content that tries to redirect it can only reach the small set of tools it was granted, which caps the blast radius. The distractors misstate the benefit: trimming tools is not primarily about speed, it does not replace isolating untrusted input, and it reduces but does not eliminate the need for approval on sensitive actions.

distractorNotes.opt-a: Plausible because fewer options can feel faster, but speed is not the security benefit; least privilege is about limiting what actions exist.
distractorNotes.opt-c: Least privilege is one layer; you still separate untrusted input from trusted instructions — the two are defense in depth, not substitutes.
distractorNotes.opt-e: A restricted tool set lowers but does not remove risk; sensitive actions can still warrant an approval step.

sourceNote: Security principles — Least privilege

stem: An internal tool exposes a 'clean up this repository' button that issues one open-ended prompt to an agent. In testing, runs vary wildly in length and cost, and one looped for a long time before stopping. How should the team make runs terminate predictably?

options.text: Give the agent a narrow objective with a clear completion test, and set a turn or spend ceiling as a backstop.
Remove any limits and let the agent decide when it is done, since a cap risks cutting off useful work midway.
Keep the broad prompt but lower reasoning effort, since cheaper turns keep the total cost of a run bounded.
Fan the broad prompt out across parallel subagents so the overall job reaches completion in less wall-clock time.

explanation: opt-a is correct: an open-ended prompt has no natural stopping point, so predictability comes from scoping the task with a verifiable completion criterion and adding a turn or budget ceiling as a safety net against runaway loops. Removing limits makes runs less predictable, lower effort trims per-turn cost but not the number of iterations, and parallelism reduces wall-clock time without bounding total work.

distractorNotes.opt-b: Plausible because caps can interrupt work, but with no stopping criterion an open-ended prompt can loop indefinitely; removing limits makes runs less predictable, not more.
distractorNotes.opt-c: Lower effort reduces cost per turn but not how many turns run, so an open-ended prompt can still run away.
distractorNotes.opt-d: Parallel subagents shorten wall-clock time but do not bound how long or how much the overall job consumes.

sourceNote: Turns and messages — running long on open-ended prompts; Turns and budget

stem: Company policy is absolute: the agent must never write to files under a secrets directory, and every attempt must be recorded. The team needs this enforced regardless of what the model decides in any given run. Where should this rule live?

options.text: In the system prompt and project memory, worded firmly so the model reliably refuses to write there.
In a lower temperature setting, so the model's tool choices become deterministic and skip the write.
In a pre-tool-use hook that inspects each call in code and blocks the ones that target the secrets directory.
In a stricter model choice, since a more capable model is better at honoring firm prohibitions in its prompt.

explanation: opt-c is correct: a hook runs deterministic code before a tool call and can deny it outright, so the policy is enforced in the harness rather than left to the model's discretion, and the same hook can log every attempt. Prompt wording and model choice only bias behavior, and temperature affects sampling, none of which guarantee a forbidden action is blocked.

distractorNotes.opt-a: Plausible because instructions usually work, but prompt and memory bias the model without guaranteeing it; an injected or determined instruction can still elicit the write.
distractorNotes.opt-b: Temperature affects sampling, not policy enforcement, and gives no guarantee a forbidden call is blocked.
distractorNotes.opt-d: Model capability is not an enforcement mechanism; no model choice deterministically prevents a specific tool call.

sourceNote: Intercept and control agent behavior with hooks — Block dangerous operations (PreToolUse)

stem: A team wants to run long-running, asynchronous agents in production but does not want to operate the sandboxes or session infrastructure those agents need. Which approach fits this constraint?

options.text: Embed the Agent SDK as a library in their own service, which runs the agent loop inside infrastructure they manage.
Call the Messages API through the Client SDK and implement the tool-execution loop within their own service.
Run the Claude Code CLI as a subprocess on their own hosts and persist each session's state to local disk.
Adopt Managed Agents, the Anthropic-hosted option that runs the agent and its sandbox so the team runs neither.

explanation: opt-d is correct: Managed Agents is a hosted product where Anthropic runs both the agent and the sandbox, which fits a team that wants long-running async agents without operating that infrastructure. The other three all keep the loop and its hosting on the team's own machines, which is precisely what they are trying to avoid.

distractorNotes.opt-a: The Agent SDK runs the loop inside your own process and infrastructure, exactly the operational burden this team wants to shed.
distractorNotes.opt-b: The Client SDK gives raw API access and pushes the entire tool loop and its hosting onto the team.
distractorNotes.opt-c: Driving the CLI still requires the team to run the hosts and manage session state themselves.

sourceNote: Compare the Agent SDK to other Claude tools — Managed Agents

stem: A product team is tempted to build a multi-step agent for a task that a single well-prompted model call with retrieval already handles accurately. According to Anthropic's guidance on building effective agents, what should guide the decision?

options.text: Build the agent anyway, because agentic systems always outperform single calls once tools are added.
Prefer the simplest solution that works, and add agentic complexity only when it demonstrably helps.
Choose a workflow rather than an agent, since a workflow is the simplest possible agentic system by definition.
Add the agent but leave its tools disabled until traffic grows, so the extra complexity stays dormant for now.

explanation: opt-b is correct: the guidance recommends finding the simplest solution and increasing complexity only when it demonstrably helps, so a single call that already works should not be replaced by an agent. Agents trade latency and cost for performance and are not always warranted, a workflow is still added complexity, and dormant complexity carries cost without benefit.

distractorNotes.opt-a: The guidance explicitly warns that agents trade latency and cost for performance and are not always the right choice.
distractorNotes.opt-c: A workflow is still added complexity; the point is to avoid an agentic system entirely when a single call suffices.
distractorNotes.opt-d: Adding dormant complexity still carries the abstraction and maintenance cost without delivering any benefit.

sourceNote: When (and when not) to use agents

stem: A team is choosing between a fixed workflow and an autonomous agent for a new feature. Select TWO statements that correctly capture the documented decision criteria.

options.text: An agent is the right choice for a well-defined task whose steps are known ahead of time and never vary.
A workflow offers predictability and consistency when the task is well-defined and its steps are known in advance.
Agents suit open-ended problems where you cannot predict the number of steps or hardcode a fixed path.
Workflows are preferable only when cost is irrelevant, since they always cost more than an equivalent agent.
The choice never depends on how far you can trust the model's decisions, only on the raw volume of requests.

explanation: opt-b and opt-c are correct: workflows give predictability for well-defined tasks with known steps, while agents fit open-ended problems where the number of steps can't be predicted and no fixed path can be hardcoded. Fixed, known steps favor a workflow not an agent, workflows are not defined by cost, and the guidance stresses you must have some trust in an agent's decision-making.

distractorNotes.opt-a: Fixed, known steps favor a workflow's predefined code paths, not an agent's dynamic, model-driven control.
distractorNotes.opt-d: Workflows are not chosen on cost; it is agent autonomy that typically raises cost, not workflows.
distractorNotes.opt-e: The guidance says you must have some level of trust in an agent's decision-making, so trust does factor into the choice.

sourceNote: When (and when not) to use agents; When to use agents

stem: A design uses one central 'manager' model call that breaks an incoming task into subtasks at runtime, hands each to a worker call, and combines the results. Select TWO statements that accurately describe this manager/supervisor structure.

options.text: The manager decides the subtasks dynamically from the input rather than from a fixed, predefined list.
The set of subtasks is fixed ahead of time, so each request follows one of a few predetermined branches.
The manager only routes work and performs no synthesis of the workers' outputs into a final result.
Because the manager handles decomposition and synthesis, each worker can focus on one narrower subtask.
Workers must execute strictly in sequence, so independent subtasks can never run concurrently here.

explanation: opt-a and opt-d are correct: in an orchestrator-workers structure the central call determines the subtasks from the specific input rather than a fixed list, and because it owns both decomposition and synthesis, each worker can concentrate on a single narrower piece. Predefined branches describe routing, the manager does synthesize results rather than merely route, and independent subtasks can run concurrently.

distractorNotes.opt-b: Predefined branches describe routing; in this pattern the subtasks are determined at runtime by the manager, not fixed.
distractorNotes.opt-c: The manager both decomposes the task and synthesizes the workers' outputs, so it is more than a router.
distractorNotes.opt-e: Independent subtasks produced by the manager can run concurrently; sequential execution is not required.

sourceNote: Workflow: Orchestrator-workers

stem: An engineering lead asks why routing parts of a large task to subagents can improve execution quality, not just throughput. Select TWO benefits that the documentation attributes to subagents.

options.text: Subagents share the parent's full conversation, so nothing has to be re-explained when work is delegated.
Each subagent runs in isolated context, so its exploratory reads don't crowd the parent's working conversation.
Independent subtasks can run in parallel, finishing in the time of the slowest rather than the sum of all.
Subagents remove the need for the parent to have any tools of its own, since they perform every action.
A subagent's intermediate tool results are merged verbatim into the parent to preserve the full detail.

explanation: opt-b and opt-c are correct: a subagent's isolated context keeps its exploratory reads out of the parent's conversation, and running independent subtasks in parallel finishes them in the time of the slowest rather than their sum. A non-fork subagent does not inherit the parent's conversation, subagents complement rather than replace the parent's tools, and only the final message returns, not intermediate results.

distractorNotes.opt-a: A non-fork subagent starts fresh and does not inherit the parent's conversation; context is deliberately isolated.
distractorNotes.opt-d: Subagents complement the parent's tools rather than removing the parent's need for tools of its own.
distractorNotes.opt-e: Only a subagent's final message returns to the parent; intermediate tool results stay isolated, which is the point.

sourceNote: Benefits of using subagents

stem: Before shipping an autonomous agent, a team reviews the tradeoffs of agent autonomy against a scripted workflow. Select TWO statements that reflect the documented guidance.

options.text: Agent autonomy is effectively free once tools exist, so cost need not factor into the decision at all.
Agents should be preferred to workflows on any task that happens to involve more than one model call.
Autonomy raises cost and risks compounding errors, so extensive testing in sandboxed environments is advised.
Because agents self-correct, guardrails add little value and can safely be dropped in trusted settings.
Agents suit open-ended problems where the needed number of steps cannot be predicted in advance.

explanation: opt-c and opt-e are correct: the guidance notes that autonomy brings higher cost and the potential for compounding errors, recommending extensive testing in sandboxed environments, and that agents fit open-ended problems where the number of steps can't be predicted. Autonomy is not free, more than one model call does not mandate an agent, and guardrails are recommended precisely because agents can compound errors.

distractorNotes.opt-a: The guidance is explicit that autonomy trades higher cost and latency for performance, so cost does matter.
distractorNotes.opt-b: Added complexity is warranted only when it demonstrably helps; multiple calls alone do not require an agent.
distractorNotes.opt-d: Guardrails are recommended alongside sandboxed testing because agents can compound errors; they are not optional.

sourceNote: Agents; When to use agents

stem: A localization feature drafts a translation, then has a second model call critique it against style and nuance guidelines and feed the critique back so the draft is revised, looping until the critique is satisfied. Which documented pattern is this?

options.text: Routing: classify the input first, then send it down a branch specialized for that category.
Parallelization using voting: run the same task several times and aggregate the separate outputs.
Evaluator-optimizer: one call drafts while another critiques in a loop until the feedback is met.
Prompt chaining: pass the input through a fixed forward sequence where each step feeds the next.

explanation: opt-c is correct: a generate-then-critique loop where one call drafts and another evaluates and feeds back until the criteria are met is the evaluator-optimizer pattern, a fit here because there are clear evaluation criteria and iterative refinement adds value. Routing branches by category, voting aggregates parallel attempts, and prompt chaining is a fixed forward sequence, none of which describe the feedback loop.

distractorNotes.opt-a: Routing classifies an input and dispatches it to a specialized branch; there is no iterative critique loop.
distractorNotes.opt-b: Voting runs the same task in parallel and aggregates outputs; it does not refine a single draft with feedback.
distractorNotes.opt-d: Prompt chaining is a fixed forward sequence of steps, not a generate-and-critique loop.

sourceNote: Workflow: Evaluator-optimizer

stem: A content pipeline writes an outline, runs a programmatic check that the outline meets set criteria, and only then writes the full document from the approved outline. Each step consumes the previous step's output in a fixed order. Which documented pattern fits?

options.text: Orchestrator-workers: a central call splits the task into subtasks decided at runtime.
Routing: classify the request and dispatch it to one of several specialized handlers.
Evaluator-optimizer: generate a draft and refine it against a critic in a repeating loop.
Prompt chaining: a fixed sequence of steps, optionally with a gate check between them.

explanation: opt-d is correct: decomposing a task into a fixed sequence where each call processes the previous one's output, with an optional programmatic gate between steps, is prompt chaining. The subtasks here are fixed and known, there is no classification into categories, and the check is a one-time gate rather than an iterative critic refining a draft.

distractorNotes.opt-a: The subtasks here are fixed and known in advance, not decomposed dynamically by a manager at runtime.
distractorNotes.opt-b: There is no classification into categories; it is one linear pipeline applied to every input.
distractorNotes.opt-c: The check is a single programmatic gate, not an iterative critic refining a draft in a loop.

sourceNote: Workflow: Prompt chaining

stem: A team maintaining a long-running agent keeps loading more reference material into its context window "just in case" it turns out to be relevant, and answer quality is slowly getting worse. Which principle should guide what actually belongs in context?

options.text: Aim for the smallest set of high-signal tokens that supports the task, because context is a finite resource and irrelevant content degrades the model's focus.
Load as much plausibly relevant material as will fit inside the window, because a fuller context reliably improves the model's overall accuracy and its recall.
Retain everything the agent has already seen so that it never has to re-derive an earlier conclusion during a later turn.
Fill the system prompt with every edge case up front, since exhaustive rules are always more dependable than concise guidance.

explanation: Anthropic's context-engineering guidance treats context as a finite resource with diminishing returns: as tokens accumulate, recall and focus degrade (context rot), so the goal is the smallest high-signal set that still fully specifies the task. Option a states exactly that. The other options assume more context is monotonically better, which is the misconception the guidance warns against; padding the window, hoarding history, or stuffing exhaustive rules all dilute the attention budget and make relevant tokens harder to use.

distractorNotes.b: This is the intuition the guidance explicitly rejects. More tokens do not reliably improve recall; beyond a point they cause context rot and reduce the model's ability to find what matters.
distractorNotes.c: Retaining all prior content indefinitely is what compaction and context editing exist to counter. Stale tool outputs and resolved turns are prime candidates for removal, not permanent retention.
distractorNotes.d: Minimal does not mean short, but exhaustively enumerating edge cases in the system prompt bloats it and buries the load-bearing instructions; curated, canonical guidance performs better.

sourceNote: Context windows — 'How the context window works' (context rot; curating what's in context)

stem: An agent runs multi-hour codebase migrations whose cumulative token count far exceeds the context window, and it must stay coherent and goal-directed across the whole task. Select THREE techniques that let it work past the window limit while preserving the context that still matters.

options.text: Raise the sampling temperature so the agent improvises whatever earlier state has scrolled out of the window.
Summarise the conversation as it nears the limit and reinitialise a fresh window from that high-fidelity summary.
Keep the entire raw message history verbatim on every turn so that no earlier detail is ever discarded.
Have the agent write structured notes to an external store and pull them back into context when they are needed later.
Delegate focused sub-tasks to sub-agents that each work in their own clean context and return only their results.
Wait for a larger context window, since a big enough window removes any need to curate what the agent sees.

explanation: For long-horizon tasks Anthropic describes three complementary techniques: compaction (summarise near the limit and continue from the summary), structured note-taking to memory outside the window that is read back later, and sub-agent architectures that isolate focused work in clean contexts. Options b, d, and e are those three. Raising temperature (a) does nothing to recover lost state; keeping all raw history (c) is precisely what causes context rot; and waiting for a bigger window (f) is rejected because windows of every size still suffer context pollution and relevance decay.

distractorNotes.a: Temperature controls randomness of sampling, not memory. It cannot restore information that has already left the window and only makes behaviour less predictable.
distractorNotes.c: Carrying the full raw history is the failure mode these techniques address; unbounded accumulation degrades recall long before any hard limit is reached.
distractorNotes.f: A larger window is not a substitute for curation. Context rot and relevance decay affect windows of all sizes, so the strongest agents still manage what they carry.

sourceNote: Context engineering for long-horizon tasks — compaction, structured note-taking, sub-agent architectures

stem: An agent works across many sessions and must remember project state, decisions, and progress that would otherwise be lost as the conversation is summarised or scrolls out of the context window. Where should that durable information live?

options.text: Entirely inside the running conversation, since anything already in the message history is guaranteed to stay available to the model.
In external notes or a file-based memory the agent writes and reads back, so the facts persist independently of the context window.
Encoded implicitly in a higher temperature setting, so the model reconstructs the missing state by improvising when it is asked.
Copied into the system prompt again on every turn, letting it grow without bound as the project accumulates more state.

explanation: Structured note-taking, or agentic memory, persists critical facts outside the context window and reads them back when needed, giving continuity across sessions and summarisation steps. That is option b. Leaving durable state only in the conversation (a) is unsafe because compaction and window limits can discard it; temperature (c) has nothing to do with memory; and endlessly appending state to the system prompt (d) bloats it and reintroduces the very window pressure you were trying to escape.

distractorNotes.a: Message history is not permanent: compaction summarises older turns and long conversations fall out of the window, so facts kept only there can silently disappear.
distractorNotes.c: Temperature governs randomness, not recall. It cannot store or retrieve state, and improvised reconstruction of prior decisions is exactly what a memory store prevents.
distractorNotes.d: Continuously growing the system prompt trades one window problem for another; persistent facts belong in an external store that is consulted on demand, not re-injected every turn.

sourceNote: Context engineering for long-horizon tasks — 'Structured note-taking' (agentic memory persisted outside the context window)

stem: A developer is deciding whether to let a long conversation keep accumulating turns or to summarise older ones as it approaches the window limit. Select TWO statements that correctly describe the tradeoff involved.

options.text: Carrying the full untrimmed history always yields better answers, because the model attends equally well to every token no matter how long the context grows.
Replacing old turns with a summary reclaims attention budget and reduces context rot, but overly aggressive summarising can drop subtle details whose importance only surfaces later.
Compaction removes any need to persist information elsewhere, since the summary is guaranteed to retain every fact the agent could later require.
Facts that must survive the whole task are more reliable when written to external notes than when left only in a conversation that may be summarised away.
Summarising conversation history is a lossless operation, so there is no real decision about what to keep versus what to discard.

explanation: Compaction distils the window into a summary so the agent can continue with a smaller, higher-signal context, but the art lies in choosing what to keep: too-aggressive compaction loses subtle context whose importance appears only later (b). Because summarisation is lossy, durable facts are safer in external notes than in a conversation that can be compacted away (d). The distractors are wrong in principle: long context is not uniformly attended (a), a summary is not a guaranteed complete record (c), and compaction is explicitly not lossless (e).

distractorNotes.a: Attention is not uniform across a long window; recall degrades as tokens accumulate, which is the whole reason to summarise rather than carry everything.
distractorNotes.c: A summary is a lossy distillation, not a guarantee. Critical facts can be dropped, which is why external persistence is recommended alongside compaction.
distractorNotes.e: Summarisation necessarily discards content, so deciding what to preserve versus drop is the central design choice, not a non-issue.

sourceNote: Context engineering for long-horizon tasks — 'Compaction' (the art of what to keep vs discard)

stem: Three separate Claude applications each need to read and update records in the same internal ticketing system, and the integration should be owned and versioned by one platform team rather than copied into each app. Which approach fits best?

options.text: Give each application its own built-in tool, relying on the fact that built-in tools can connect to almost any internal system without any extra integration work.
Embed the ticketing access logic directly in every application's system prompt so each app carries and maintains its own copy of it.
Build an MCP server exposing the ticketing operations as tools, so every application connects to one integration that one team maintains independently.
Paste the latest ticket records into each request's context so the applications always appear to have current data to work from.

explanation: An MCP server exposes reusable tools that multiple Claude applications can share and that can be maintained and versioned independently of any one app, which is exactly the reuse-plus-single-owner requirement here (c). Built-in tools do not automatically reach arbitrary internal APIs (a); duplicating logic across system prompts is neither reusable nor centrally maintainable (b); and pasting data gives no live read/update capability and wastes context (d).

distractorNotes.a: Built-in tools are a fixed Anthropic-provided set and do not connect to an arbitrary internal REST service, so this misstates what they can do.
distractorNotes.b: Copying the integration into each prompt is the opposite of single-owner reuse; three divergent copies become three maintenance burdens.
distractorNotes.d: Pasted records are a static snapshot with no ability to update the system, and they consume context on every request without providing live access.

sourceNote: Connect Claude Code to tools via MCP — MCP servers give access to your tools, databases, and APIs, reusable across applications

stem: A developer keeps pasting the same multi-step release checklist into Claude Code at the start of every deployment session. They want the procedure available on demand without carrying it in every conversation. What should they create?

options.text: A new MCP server whose single job is to return the fixed checklist text over the network whenever the deployment session happens to ask for it.
A custom API tool that does nothing but echo the fixed checklist steps back into the model's context on request.
A permanent block in the system prompt holding the whole checklist so it is loaded on absolutely every turn.
A Skill that stores the checklist as instructions and loads into context only when the procedure is actually relevant.

explanation: A Skill is exactly for a repeated procedure or checklist: its body loads only when relevant, so the long reference costs almost nothing until it is needed (d). Standing up an MCP server (a) or a custom tool (b) to serve static text is heavy over-engineering for content that has no external system behind it, and pinning the checklist in the system prompt (c) pays its full token cost on every single turn.

distractorNotes.a: MCP is for connecting to external systems and data; wrapping a static checklist in a networked server adds infrastructure with no live integration to justify it.
distractorNotes.b: A custom tool implies real execution against a system. Using one merely to re-emit fixed text is unnecessary machinery for what is just reusable instructions.
distractorNotes.c: Putting the checklist in the system prompt loads it every turn even when no deployment is happening, which is the context bloat a Skill is designed to avoid.

sourceNote: Extend Claude with skills — a skill's body loads only when used; create one for a repeated multi-step procedure

stem: A team is matching several capabilities to the right customization approach among built-in tools, custom tools, Skills, and MCP servers. Select THREE statements that correctly pair a use case with an approach.

options.text: Built-in tools are the right default for any private internal REST service, because they can reach any such endpoint with no extra integration.
An MCP server fits when a capability must be shared across several applications and maintained independently of any one of them.
An MCP server should be chosen for every integration, since prompts and Skills are unable to trigger any external system at all.
A Skill fits when a repeated multi-step procedure should be packaged as reusable instructions that load only when they are relevant.
A Skill is the right choice whenever you need live authenticated access to an external database on every single request.
A custom tool fits when the application itself must execute a specific action against your own system that no built-in tool covers.

explanation: The correct pairings follow each approach's purpose: MCP for a capability shared and independently maintained across apps (b), a Skill for a reusable multi-step procedure that loads on demand (d), and a custom tool for an app-specific action against your own system with no built-in equivalent (f). The distractors misstate scope: built-in tools do not reach arbitrary internal APIs (a); MCP is not mandatory for every integration and Skills can drive tools (c); and live per-request database access is a job for a tool or MCP server, not a Skill (e).

distractorNotes.a: Built-in tools are a fixed set and do not automatically connect to arbitrary private endpoints, so they are not a universal default for internal services.
distractorNotes.c: This overstates MCP's necessity and wrongly claims Skills cannot invoke external systems; the choice depends on reuse and ownership, not an absolute rule.
distractorNotes.e: Skills package instructions that load on demand; they are not the mechanism for live authenticated data access, which belongs to a tool or an MCP server.

sourceNote: Extend Claude with skills; compare with MCP servers and plugins for selecting the appropriate approach

stem: A single application needs Claude to run one specific transformation on values the app already holds, with no external system involved and no reuse expected anywhere else. Considering built-in tools, custom tools, Skills, and MCP servers, which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Implement it as a custom tool in the application, since the action is local, specific, and does not need to be shared or independently maintained.
Stand up a dedicated MCP server for the transformation so that it could in theory be reused later, even though no other application is expected to ever consume it.
Package it as a Skill so the steps load on demand, even though this is one deterministic computation rather than a reusable procedure.
Assume a built-in tool already covers this application-specific computation and wire the app to call that instead of writing anything.

explanation: Guidance is to choose the simplest approach that fits and add complexity only when needed. A local, single-app action with no external system and no reuse is precisely what a custom tool is for (a). An MCP server (b) adds shared infrastructure for reuse that will never happen; a Skill (c) is for reusable procedures, not a single computation; and there is no built-in tool for arbitrary app-specific logic (d), so relying on one is misplaced.

distractorNotes.b: MCP earns its overhead when a capability is shared and independently maintained. Building a server for a one-app, no-reuse action is over-engineering.
distractorNotes.c: Skills package multi-step procedures that load when relevant; a single deterministic transformation is not that shape and gains nothing from being a Skill.
distractorNotes.d: Built-in tools are a fixed set and do not cover arbitrary application-specific computation, so assuming one exists leaves the requirement unmet.

sourceNote: When (and when not) to use agents — find the simplest solution and add complexity only when needed

stem: A developer has fixed, standing instructions that should govern the assistant's role and behaviour on every request, alongside per-request user content that varies. Where should the standing instructions be placed?

options.text: Appended to the end of each user message, so they always sit as close as possible to where the model begins its response.
In the system prompt, which is designed to carry persistent role and behaviour instructions that apply consistently across all turns.
Split unpredictably between the system prompt and user turns so the model encounters the same rules from several positions.
Only in the first user turn, relying on the model to carry those rules forward unaided through the rest of the conversation.

explanation: The system prompt is the component meant to hold persistent role and behavioural instructions that apply across the whole conversation, so standing instructions belong there (b). Appending them to every user message (a) mixes durable rules with variable input and duplicates them needlessly; scattering them (c) is inconsistent and hard to maintain; and relying on a single early user turn (d) leaves the rules vulnerable to being summarised or drifting out of focus over a long session.

distractorNotes.a: Repeating standing rules in every user turn conflates persistent behaviour with per-request content and wastes tokens; the system prompt exists precisely so you do not have to.
distractorNotes.c: Randomly splitting instructions across components makes the prompt inconsistent and hard to reason about, without improving adherence.
distractorNotes.d: A single early user turn is not durable; over a long or compacted conversation those instructions can lose salience or drop out of the window entirely.

sourceNote: Prompting best practices — giving Claude a role via the system prompt for persistent behaviour

stem: A developer is struggling to get consistent output formatting from an assistant and is iterating on the prompt. Select THREE techniques that Anthropic recommends for steering output format.

options.text: Raise the sampling temperature so that the model adheres to the requested output format more strictly and predictably.
Tell the model what to do rather than what not to do, for example describing the prose you want instead of forbidding markdown.
Prefill a partial assistant message to force the format, which remains the recommended formatting technique on the current models.
Use XML tags or explicit format indicators to mark where a particular kind of output should be placed in the response.
State the formatting rule once and never revisit it, since iterating on the wording of a prompt rarely changes the output.
Match the style of the prompt to the desired output, since the formatting used in the prompt influences the response's formatting.

explanation: The recommended levers for output formatting are: state what to do instead of what to avoid (b), use XML tags or format indicators to delineate output (d), and match your prompt's style to the output you want (f). Temperature (a) governs randomness, not format adherence; prefilling (c) is no longer supported on current 4.6-and-later models and returns an error; and refusing to iterate (e) contradicts the core practice of iterative refinement.

distractorNotes.a: Temperature affects randomness of sampling, not whether the model follows a format. It is not a formatting control.
distractorNotes.c: Prefilled assistant responses are unsupported on current models and return a 400 error; structured outputs or explicit instructions replace that technique.
distractorNotes.e: Iterative refinement is central to prompt engineering; adjusting wording and examples based on failures is how formatting reliability improves.

sourceNote: Prompting best practices — 'Control the format of responses' (say what to do; XML indicators; match prompt style)

stem: When a client tool fails, a developer currently returns a tool result whose entire content is the word "failed". Claude then stalls or apologises instead of recovering. According to Anthropic's tool guidance, what is the better design for the error content returned to the model?

options.text: Return an empty result with no explanation so the model is not distracted by the failure and simply proceeds with the turn.
Suppress the error entirely and silently retry the identical call in a tight loop until it eventually happens to succeed.
Return a message stating what went wrong and what to try next, so the model has the context it needs to recover or adapt.
Return the raw low-level stack trace verbatim, on the basis that more internal detail is always more useful to the model.

explanation: Guidance is to write instructive error messages: instead of a generic "failed", say what went wrong and what Claude should try next, so it can recover or adapt without guessing (c). An empty result (a) hides the failure and gives nothing to act on; silently retrying forever (b) removes the model from the loop and can hang; and dumping a raw stack trace (d) is low-signal noise, not the actionable guidance the model needs.

distractorNotes.a: An empty result leaves the model unaware of what failed and unable to adjust, which is how it ends up stalling in the first place.
distractorNotes.b: Blind unbounded retries mask the real problem and can loop indefinitely; the model should be told about the failure so it can choose an alternative.
distractorNotes.d: A verbatim stack trace is high-volume, low-signal context; a concise statement of the cause and next step is far more actionable for the model.

sourceNote: Handling errors with is_error — write instructive error messages describing what went wrong and what to try next

stem: A team is designing the tool set for an agent that spans several internal services and keeps mis-selecting tools and passing over-large results back into context. Select THREE tool-set construction practices Anthropic recommends.

options.text: Create one narrowly scoped tool per action so the surface is as large and finely granular as it can possibly be.
Consolidate related operations into a single tool with an action parameter rather than many near-identical tools.
Rely on the model to disambiguate heavily overlapping tools, on the assumption that adding more tools always improves coverage.
Namespace tool names by service or resource so that tool selection stays unambiguous as the library grows larger.
Return every field the backend produces in each response, so that the model can never be short of information.
Shape responses to return only high-signal fields and stable identifiers instead of bloated, opaque payloads.

explanation: The recommended practices are consolidating related operations behind an action parameter (b), namespacing tool names by service so selection stays unambiguous (d), and returning only high-signal fields and stable identifiers (f). The distractors invert each of these: a sprawling one-tool-per-action surface (a) and piling on overlapping tools (c) increase selection ambiguity, and returning every backend field (e) bloats context and buries what matters.

distractorNotes.a: A maximally granular surface of near-identical tools is what causes the mis-selection described; guidance is to consolidate, not proliferate.
distractorNotes.c: If a human cannot say which overlapping tool applies, the model cannot either; more tools do not automatically help and often hurt selection.
distractorNotes.e: Returning every field wastes context and makes it harder for the model to extract the signal; responses should be trimmed to what is needed.

sourceNote: Define tools — 'Best practices for tool definitions' (consolidate operations, namespacing, high-signal responses)

stem: An agent that reads untrusted third-party content can also call tools that move money and delete records. The team wants to bound the damage if an injected instruction ever slips past their screening. Which design principle matters most?

options.text: Raise the model's temperature so that its behaviour is harder for an attacker crafting an injection to anticipate and steer.
Add a single system-prompt sentence telling the model never to obey malicious instructions, and treat that one sentence as the application's primary control.
Grant the agent broad permissions so that, if an injection does succeed, it retains enough access to clean up the damage itself.
Apply least privilege and require authorization or human confirmation before sensitive actions, so model output alone cannot trigger irreversible ones.

explanation: Because a successful injection acts through the model's output, the durable defense is to break the link between that output and privileged action: apply least privilege and gate sensitive or irreversible operations behind authorization or human confirmation (d). Temperature (a) is irrelevant to injection; a single system-prompt sentence (b) is not an enforceable boundary on its own; and broad permissions (c) do the opposite of containment by maximising what a successful injection can reach.

distractorNotes.a: Randomising outputs does nothing to stop an injection from invoking a dangerous tool and only makes behaviour less predictable overall.
distractorNotes.b: Prompt-level instructions help but are not an enforceable control; they can be overridden and must be backed by least-privilege and confirmation gates.
distractorNotes.c: Broad permissions widen the blast radius; the goal is to minimise what a compromised turn can do, not to give it more power to act.

sourceNote: Indirect prompt injection — 'Limit Claude's access to sensitive data and actions' (least privilege)

stem: A public-facing assistant is the target of users who deliberately craft inputs to bypass its guardrails. Select THREE mitigations Anthropic recommends against these direct jailbreak attempts.

options.text: Raise the model temperature so that manipulative prompts become harder for the attacker to reproduce reliably across attempts.
Pre-screen incoming user input with a lightweight model that classifies it for harmful intent before it reaches the main conversation.
Add a line politely asking users not to submit malicious instructions and treat that request as a sufficient guardrail on its own.
Throttle or ban users who repeatedly trigger the same guardrail refusals after being told their actions violate the usage policy.
Switch to a larger model on the assumption that larger models are inherently immune to jailbreak attempts.
Harden the system prompt so it states the ethical and legal boundaries and tells the model exactly how it should refuse.

explanation: For direct jailbreaks, where the user is the adversary, the recommended layers are a lightweight harmlessness screen on input (b), responding to repeat offenders by throttling or banning them (d), and hardening the system prompt with explicit boundaries and refusal guidance (f). The distractors are ineffective: temperature (a) does not deter manipulation, a polite request (c) is not an enforceable control, and a larger model (e) is not inherently immune and can even be more susceptible.

distractorNotes.a: Temperature changes randomness, not resistance to manipulation; it is not a guardrail against crafted jailbreak inputs.
distractorNotes.c: A polite instruction is unenforceable and trivially ignored by a determined adversary; it cannot substitute for screening and hardened prompts.
distractorNotes.e: Model size does not confer immunity to jailbreaks, and a more instruction-following model can be more, not less, susceptible to manipulation.

sourceNote: Jailbreaks and direct prompt injection — harmlessness screens, respond to repeat offenders, prompt engineering

stem: A service asks Claude for JSON and parses the reply. Roughly one call in twenty fails to parse, so the team wrapped the call in a retry loop that reissues the request until parsing succeeds. Costs and latency have both climbed. What is the better approach?

options.text: Raise the temperature so that a failed attempt is more likely to produce different output on the next try, which shortens the retry loop.
Keep the retry loop but strip the reply of any text outside the outermost braces first, since the parse failures are formatting noise.
Constrain the response with structured outputs, so the reply is schema-compliant by construction and the retry loop can be removed entirely.
Move the schema into the system prompt and restate it before every user turn, so the instruction stays close to the point of generation.

explanation: Structured outputs constrain generation to a supplied JSON schema, so the response is valid and correctly typed by construction rather than by luck. That removes the failure the retry loop exists to absorb, along with the duplicated cost and latency of reissuing requests. The other options all treat the symptom: they try to make an unconstrained generation fail less often, rather than removing the possibility of a schema violation.

distractorNotes.opt-a: Temperature does change sampling, but it is not a correctness control. Varying the output distribution to make a malformed reply less likely still leaves the reply unconstrained.
distractorNotes.opt-b: Salvaging text around the JSON is a real defensive technique, but here it papers over a problem that can be eliminated outright, and it silently accepts whatever survives the strip.
distractorNotes.opt-d: Restating a schema in the prompt is instruction, not enforcement. The model is still free to deviate, so the parse failures continue at some lower rate.

sourceNote: Structured outputs — constrained decoding guarantees schema-compliant responses, removing the need for retries on schema violations

stem: A summarisation endpoint occasionally stores summaries that end mid-sentence. The integration reads the first text block of every successful response and writes it straight to the database. No errors are logged. What is the underlying defect?

options.text: The client never inspects why generation stopped, so a response cut short by the output limit is stored as though it were complete.
The client is reading the first text block rather than concatenating every block, so any summary split across blocks is stored truncated.
The database column is too narrow for the longer summaries, so the value is silently cut to length as it is written rather than rejected.
The requests are being served without streaming, so any summary longer than a single response chunk is delivered incomplete to the client.

explanation: A response that hits the output token limit is still a successful, well-formed response. The signal that it was cut short lives in the stop reason, which distinguishes a turn that finished naturally from one that ran out of room, was refused, or paused. Consuming output defensively means branching on that signal before treating text as final, which is exactly the step this integration skips.

distractorNotes.opt-b: Worth doing, and a real source of bugs, but it would drop whole segments rather than produce text that stops mid-sentence at varying lengths.
distractorNotes.opt-c: Plausible, but a storage-layer truncation is a property of the database rather than the integration, and the symptom would track the column width rather than the generation.
distractorNotes.opt-d: Streaming changes how output is delivered, not how much of it is generated. A non-streamed response carries the full generated text.

sourceNote: Handling stop reasons — a successful response may have ended because the output limit was reached, and clients should branch on the stop reason

stem: A team is hardening the code that consumes Claude's output before an audit. Select TWO practices that genuinely improve robustness rather than merely appearing to.

options.text: Treat a schema-valid response as verified, since constrained generation has already established that the content is correct.
Validate the meaning of the output against business rules, because a guarantee about shape says nothing about whether the values are right.
Log the raw response alongside the parsed result, so a later dispute can be traced to what the model actually returned.
Discard any response the parser rejects without recording it, to keep malformed content out of the audit trail entirely.
Infer confidence from how assertively the response is phrased, and route the least hedged answers through review.

explanation: Constrained generation guarantees that output parses and that fields carry the declared types, and nothing beyond that. A well-formed response can still be wrong, so semantic validation against business rules remains the caller's job. Retaining the raw response next to the parsed result is what makes a failure investigable after the fact, which is precisely what an audit needs.

distractorNotes.opt-a: This is the error the skill is named for. Schema compliance is a structural guarantee; it is silent on whether the values are accurate.
distractorNotes.opt-d: Exactly inverts the goal. The rejected responses are the most diagnostic evidence available, and discarding them removes the audit trail rather than protecting it.
distractorNotes.opt-e: Assertive phrasing is not a confidence signal. Fluent, confident wording accompanies wrong answers as readily as right ones, so routing on tone selects almost arbitrarily.

sourceNote: Structured outputs — the stated guarantees are schema-level: valid JSON, guaranteed field types and required fields

stem: An agent calls an internal pricing tool. The team needs certainty that the arguments Claude passes to that tool always match the tool's declared input schema, because a malformed argument reaches a downstream billing system. Which approach fits the requirement?

options.text: Describe the argument format carefully in the tool description and add examples of well-formed calls, so the model has a pattern to copy.
Constrain the assistant's final text response to a JSON schema, which covers the arguments because tool calls are emitted as part of that response.
Accept the call, submit it to the billing system, and roll the transaction back if the billing system rejects the argument as malformed.
Enable strict tool use, so the tool name and its inputs are themselves schema-validated during generation rather than checked afterwards.

explanation: Structured outputs cover two distinct surfaces. Constraining the response format governs the text Claude returns; strict tool use governs the tool name and the inputs Claude passes. The requirement here is about tool arguments, so it is the tool-use surface that must be constrained. Choosing between the two is a matter of knowing which part of the exchange each one governs.

distractorNotes.opt-a: Good tool descriptions genuinely raise the hit rate, but description is guidance rather than enforcement, and the requirement asks for certainty.
distractorNotes.opt-b: Confuses the two surfaces. Constraining the response format does not govern tool inputs, so the malformed arguments would still pass through.
distractorNotes.opt-c: Pushes validation past the boundary it was supposed to protect. The billing system is the thing being shielded, so letting it perform the check defeats the purpose.

sourceNote: Structured outputs — strict tool use guarantees schema validation on tool names and inputs, complementing JSON output formats

stem: A nightly job that extracts fields from documents has started failing. On some runs the API returns a client error before the model is invoked; on others the call succeeds but the extracted values are wrong. An engineer wants to isolate where the fault lies before changing anything. What best separates the two cases?

options.text: Rerun the failures at a lower temperature, and treat anything that then succeeds as a model problem and anything that still fails as an integration problem.
Separate failures the API rejected as invalid requests from calls that returned successfully, since the first class is the integration layer and the second is the output.
Compare the failure rate against the previous week, and treat any increase as a service-side regression that should be raised with the provider.
Retry every failure with backoff, and treat the ones that eventually succeed as transient so that only the permanent failures need investigation.

explanation: The two failure classes have different origins and different fixes. A request the API refuses never reached generation, so the fault is in how the integration assembled the call. A call that returns successfully but with wrong content did reach generation, so the fault lies in the prompt, the context supplied, or the handling of the output. Sorting by that boundary tells the engineer which half of the system to open first.

distractorNotes.opt-a: Sampling settings affect only the generation half, so this diagnoses nothing about requests that were rejected before generation, and it conflates non-determinism with a defect.
distractorNotes.opt-c: Rate comparison detects that something changed without indicating where, and it prematurely attributes the change to the provider rather than to the caller.
distractorNotes.opt-d: Backoff is the right response to transient errors once identified, but it treats a whole mixed population as transient and hides the invalid requests it silently retries.

sourceNote: Errors — request-level errors such as invalid_request_error are raised against the caller's request, distinct from a successful response whose content is unsatisfactory

stem: A platform team must guarantee that Claude Code never runs a command that deletes a production database, whatever the session or the prompt. They plan to enforce this with a hook. Where in the lifecycle must the check run, and why?

options.text: At session start, where the hook can scan the configured tool list once and refuse to open a session that exposes any destructive command.
On every user prompt submission, where the hook can reject any prompt whose wording suggests the user is asking for a destructive operation.
Before each tool call, where the hook receives the pending call and can deny it, so the command never executes in the first place.
After each tool call, where the hook sees exactly what ran and can raise an alert and begin restoring from the most recent backup.

explanation: A guardrail against a destructive action has to sit between the decision to act and the action itself. The pre-tool-use event fires on every tool call inside the agentic loop and receives the pending call, so the handler can inspect the actual command and deny it before execution. The other placements either run too early to see the concrete call or too late to prevent it.

distractorNotes.opt-a: Runs once, before any call exists. It can reason about what is available in principle but never sees the specific command, and a broadly capable tool cannot be judged in advance.
distractorNotes.opt-b: Filters intent rather than action, so it misses any destructive call the model arrives at from an innocuous request, which is the case that most needs catching.
distractorNotes.opt-d: Fires after execution. Detection and recovery are valuable, but the requirement is prevention, and by this point the deletion has already happened.

sourceNote: Hooks reference — hook lifecycle: PreToolUse and PostToolUse fire on every tool call inside the agentic loop, and a handler can inspect the input and return a decision
